, and both of these words are
losing
.
∎

Remark 39
.

The previous lemma applies, in particular, to
\omega
-regular closed
objectives. We did not need to add
progress consistency
as an hypothesis in Proposition
35
, as this property is granted for
closed
objective by Lemma
19
.

We are now ready to move on to the characterisation of
\omega
-regular open
objectives.

Open objectives

We now study the dual of
closed objectives
, namely,
open
ones.
Let
L\subseteq\Sigma^{*}
.
The
reachability objective associated to
L
is defined by

\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}\mathsf{Reach}(L)}=\{w\in\Sigma^{\omega}\mid w\text{ contains a prefix in }L\}.

An objective
W
is
topologically open
if
W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Reach}(L)}
for some
L\subseteq\Sigma^{*}
. (These are the open subsets of
\Sigma^{\omega}
for the Cantor topology.)
Similarly to the previous subsection, we define the class of
\omega
-regular open objectives
as those that are both
open
and
\omega
-regular
.

Remark 40
.

An open objective
W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Reach}(L)}
is
\omega
-regular
if and only if
L
is a regular language of finite words if and only if
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is finite.

Let us state a characterisation of
positionality
for
\omega
-regular open
objectives.
Characterisations for the full classes of
open
and
closed
objectives (without
\omega
-regularity
assumptions) will be obtained in Section
8
.

Proposition 41

(Positionality for open objectives)
.

An
\omega
-regular open
objective
W
is
positional
if and only if it is
progress consistent
and its set of
residuals

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is totally ordered.

Necessity follows from combining Lemmas
33
and
38
; we omit a proof of sufficiency in this warm-up.
In particular, we obtain the following corollary of Propositions
35
and
41
.

Corollary 42
.

Any
positional

\omega
-regular open
objective is
bipositional
.

We now give an example of an objective that satisfies the requirement from the previous proposition.

Example 43

(Positional open objective)
.

Consider the
\omega
-regular open
objective

W_{n}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Reach}((a\Sigma^{*})^{n})}.

It was introduced (for
n=2
) in
[
4
, Lemma 13]
as an example of a
bipositional

objective
which is not
concave
(that is, no shuffle of two words outside
W
belongs to
W
; see
[
34
, Def 4.2]
for details).
Its
residuals
are given by

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\varepsilon}^{-1}W<{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}a}^{-1}W<{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(aa)}^{-1}W<\dots<{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(a^{n})}^{-1}W=\Sigma^{\omega},

which are totally ordered.
Moreover, for any
residual class

[a^{i}]
with
i<n
, we have
[a^{i}]<[a^{i}u]
if and only if
u
contains the letter
a
, in which case
a^{i}u^{\omega}\in W
.
Therefore,
W
is
progress consistent
, so we conclude that it is
bipositional
.

Many natural examples of objectives are in fact
prefix-independent
; for those, the two conditions about the
residuals
above are trivially satisfied.
Yet, this does not suffice to guarantee their positionality.
We continue our introductory exploration with objectives recognised by
deterministic

Büchi automata
.

4.3
Büchi recognisable objectives: Uniformity of
0
-transitions

Our goal in this section is to present another property of
positional

\omega
-regular objectives
, namely, that they can be
recognised
by a
deterministic

parity automaton

\mathcal{A}
in which
0
-transitions
are
uniform over
each
residual class
:

For any
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{\mathcal{A}}}q^{\prime}
and
a\in\Sigma
, if
q\xrightarrow{a:0}
then
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:0}
.

In our main induction (Section
5.2
), we will derive a similar property for all even
priorities
.
To illustrate the technique, we now only focus on the case of
Büchi recognisable
languages, which helps alleviate some of the technicalities while preserving the important ideas behind the proof.
On the way, we characterise
positionality
for these objectives, reobtaining the main result of
[
9
]
.

The proof is split into two parts: first, we focus on the
prefix-independent
case, and then reduce to it.

Prefix-independent Büchi recognisable objectives

It is well-known that
Büchi languages
are
positional

[
29
]
, that is, those of the form

\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}\mathsf{Buchi}_{\Sigma}(B)}=\{w\in\Sigma^{\omega}\mid\text{ letters of }B\text{ appear infinitely often in }w\}.

We prove now that these are the only
positional

prefix-independent

Büchi recognisable
objectives.
Our proof considerably simplifies that of
[
9
]
.

Proposition 44

(
[
9
, Proposition 11]
)
.

A
prefix-independent

Büchi recognisable

W
is
positional
if and only if it is a
Büchi language
.

In particular, Proposition
44
tells us that there is a
Büchi automaton
with just one state
recognising

W
. In this automaton,
0
-transitions
are trivially
uniform
.

Super words and super letters.

We say that
u\in\Sigma^{+}
is a
super word
(for
W
) if, for every
w\in\Sigma^{\omega}
, if
w
contains
u
infinitely often as a factor, then
w\in W
.
If
u
is a letter, we say that it is a
super letter
.
Let
\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}B}_{W}\subseteq\Sigma
be the set of
super letters
for
W
. It is clear that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Buchi}_{\Sigma}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}B}_{W})}\subseteq W
. We will show that, if
W
is
positional
, this is in fact an equality.

Lemma 45

(Existence of super letters)
.

A non-empty
prefix-independent

positional
objective
W

recognised
by a
deterministic

Büchi automaton
admits a
super letter
.

One may easily deduce Proposition
44
from Lemma
45
: the restriction
W^{\prime}
of
W
to
non-super letters
is a
prefix-independent

Büchi recognisable

positional
objective which contains no
super letter
. Thus, Lemma
45
tells us that
W^{\prime}=\emptyset
and therefore
W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Buchi}_{\Sigma}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}B}_{W})}
.

Proof of Lemma
45
.

Fix a non-empty
prefix-independent

positional
objective
W

recognised
by a
deterministic

Büchi automaton

\mathcal{A}
, and assume without loss of generality that
\mathcal{A}
is strongly connected (thus, every state can be chosen initial) and in
normal form
.
Since
W
is non-empty, note that
\mathcal{A}
must contain a transition with
priority

0
.
We will use the following observation.

Claim 46

(Super words in Büchi automata)
.

A word
w\in\Sigma^{+}
is a
super word
if and only if for all states
q
of
\mathcal{A}
,
priority

0
appears on the path
q\mathrel{\hbox to22.88pt{\vbox to9.92pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 11.44218pt\lower-5.50832pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}
{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{

.

A game
\mathcal{G}
in which

infinitely often, but in which she cannot
win
using a
positional strategy
.

Positionality for Büchi recognisable objectives

We now state a characterisation of
positionality
for all
Büchi recognisable
objectives, without assuming
prefix-independence
.

Proposition 49

(Positionality of Büchi recognisable objectives
[
9
, Theorem 10]
)
.

Let
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
be a
Büchi recognisable

objective
. Then,
W
is
positional
if and only if:

•

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is totally ordered,

•

W
is
progress consistent
, and

•

W
can be
recognised
by a
Büchi automaton

on top of
the
automaton of residuals
.

Example 50

(Positional Büchi recognisable objective
[
9
, Example 7]
)
.

Over the alphabet
\Sigma=\{a,b\}
, let

W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathtt{Inf}}(a)\cup{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Reach}(aa)},

that is, a word
w\in\Sigma^{\omega}
belongs to
W
if either it contains letter
a
infinitely often, or it contains the factor
aa
at some point.
This objective has three different
residuals
,

[\varepsilon]<[a]<[aa]=\Sigma^{\omega}.

Figure
9
depicts a deterministic
Büchi automaton
defined on top of the
residual automaton
of
W
.
It is easy to verify that this objective is
progress consistent
, so by Proposition
49
, it is a positional objective.

Figure 9:
Büchi automaton

recognising
the objective
W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathtt{Inf}}(a)\cup{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Reach}(aa)}
.

As earlier, we focus on explaining the necessity of the conditions from Proposition
49
, and we omit a proof of sufficiency in this warm-up. We already know that the two first conditions are necessary (Lemmas
33
and
38
).
We now present the techniques used to obtain the necessity of the third condition.

Uniformity of
0
-transitions for positional objectives

Our objective is to derive the following result.

Lemma 51

(Uniform behaviour of
0
-transitions)
.

Let
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
be a
positional

Büchi recognisable
language.
There is a
deterministic

Büchi automaton

\mathcal{A}

recognising

W
such that for every pair
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{\mathcal{A}}}q^{\prime}
of equivalent states and for every letter
a
, transition
q\xrightarrow{a}
produces
priority

0
if and only if transition
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a}
produces
priority

0
.

Necessity of the conditions from Proposition
49
easily follows. In fact, what the previous lemma tells us is that we can take the
quotient automaton

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\sim_{\mathcal{A}}$}}\right.}}
and assign priorities to its transitions consistently.

The techniques we now introduce for proving Lemma
51
will be extended in our main induction (Section
5.2
).
The idea is to reduce to the
prefix-independent
case, captured by Proposition
44
. For this, we associate a
prefix-independent
language, over an ad-hoc alphabet, to each
residual
of the objective under consideration.

For the rest of this part of the section, we fix a
positional
objective
W

recognised
by a
deterministic

Büchi automaton

\mathcal{A}
.

Localising to a residual.

For each
residual class

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[u]}
of
W
, we define the
local alphabet at
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[u]}
as:

\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}\Sigma}_{[u]}=\{w\in\Sigma^{+}\mid{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[uw]}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[u]}\text{ and for any proper prefix }w^{\prime}\text{ of }w,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[uw^{\prime}]}\neq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[u]}\}.

Note that, if it is non-empty,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[u]}
is a
prefix code
, and therefore it is a
uniquely decodable alphabet
.
Note that in general
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[u]}
may be infinite, however this is completely harmless in this context, and we will freely allow ourselves to talk about automata over infinite alphabets.
5
5

5

Note that in a finite automata over an infinite alphabet, there are finitely many classes of letters such that two letters from the same class admit exactly the same transitions. Hence one may easily turn such automata into automata over finite alphabets.
Also,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[u]}
is possibly empty; in the following definitions we assume that this is not the case.

Seeing words in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[u]}^{\omega}
as words in
\Sigma^{\omega}
, define the
localisation of
W
to
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[u]}
to be the objective

\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}W_{[u]}}=\{w\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[u]}^{\omega}\mid uw\in W\}.

Observe that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{[u]}}
is
prefix-independent
. Moreover it is
positional
: any
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{[u]}}
-game
in which
Eve
could not
play optimally using positional strategies
would provide a counterexample for the
positionality
of
W
.

For a state
q
of a
Büchi automaton

\mathcal{A}

recognising

W
, define
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[q]}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{[q]}}
in the natural way:
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[q]}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[u]}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{[q]}}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{[u]}}
for
u
a word that reaches
q
from the
initial state
.
Observe that a word
w\in\Sigma^{*}
belongs to
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[q]}^{*}
if and only if it connects states in the class
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]}
. Elements in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[q]}
are those that do not pass twice through this class.
We remark that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[q]}\neq\emptyset
if and only if
q
is a
recurrent
state (it belongs to some non-trivial
SCC
).

Let
q
be a
recurrent
state. The
local automaton of the residual
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]}
is the
Büchi automaton

\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}\mathcal{A}}_{[q]}
defined as:

•

The set of states is
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]}
.

•

The initial state is arbitrary.

•

For
w\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[q]}
,
q\xrightarrow{w:x}q^{\prime}
if
q\mathrel{\hbox to23.43pt{\vbox to8.42pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 11.71649pt\lower-4.7597pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}
{{}}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{}{}{{
{}{}}}{
{}{}}

We say that the automaton

Remark 52
.

If
\mathcal{A}
is
polished
and
q
is a
transient
state, then, it is the only state in its
residual class
:
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]}=\{q\}
.
We will apply the term
recurrent
(resp.
transient
) to a class
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]}
if
q
is
recurrent
(resp.
transient
). This is well defined by the previous comment.

Lemma 53

(Obtaining a
polished
automata)
.

Any
positional

Büchi recognisable
language
W
can be
recognised
by a
polished

deterministic

Büchi automaton
.

Proof.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a
deterministic

Büchi automaton

recognising

W
.
We will first
polish
the
residual class

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]}
of a fixed state
q
.
Consider the restriction
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}}_{[q]}^{\prime}
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}}_{[q]}
to transitions labelled with
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}N}_{[q]}
, and take
S_{[q]}
to be a final SCC of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}}_{[q]}^{\prime}
; without loss of generality we assume that
q\in S_{[q]}
.

Now consider the automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
obtained from
\mathcal{A}
by removing states in
[q]\setminus S_{[q]}
, and
redirecting
transitions that go to
[q]\setminus S_{[q]}
in
\mathcal{A}
to transitions towards
q
producing
priority

0
.
Note that this transformation
preserves the residuals
: if
p_{1}\xrightarrow{a}p_{2}
in
\mathcal{A}
and
p_{1}\xrightarrow{a}p_{2}^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
, then
p_{2}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{\mathcal{A}}}p_{2}^{\prime}
. Also, either
|\mathcal{A}^{\prime}|<|\mathcal{A}|
, or
\mathcal{A}
is left unchanged.
We now prove that it preserves the language.

.
Together, the facts that

•

(aw)^{\omega}\notin{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}_{q}})}

•

, and

•

prove that Eve wins the game on the right of Figure
10
, but not
positionally
.

Figure 10:
On the left, the situation in the automaton
\mathcal{A}
. We have the equivalences
q_{1}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{\mathcal{A}}}q_{2}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{\mathcal{A}}}q^{\prime}
and

. On the right, a game where

can

but not

.

Thus we proved that if
W
is a
Büchi recognisable

positional
objective, it can be
recognised
by a
Büchi automaton
in which
0
-transitions

behave uniformly
.
By extending the technique from this section, we will show in Section
5.2
that this property (and its generalisation to all even priorities) also holds for automata using higher
priorities
.

4.4
Objectives recognised by coBüchi automata: Total order given by safe languages

We now consider
coBüchi recognisable
objectives.
Our analysis requires using
history-deterministic
automata and techniques from
[
1
]
.

Most of the section is devoted to the case of
prefix-independent
objectives, for which we propose a characterisation of
positionality
(Proposition
60
).
At the end of the section, we comment on how to extend this characterisation to any
coBüchi recognisable
objective (Proposition
69
).
In the spirit of this warm-up, we omit proofs of sufficiency.

Prefix-independent coBüchi recognisable objectives

Let us start by introducing some terminology relative to
coBüchi automata
. Our analysis requires considering
automata
that are not necessarily
deterministic
, however, we have a fine control of the non-determinism that will appear.
First, all automata in this subsection will be
history-deterministic
.
Moreover, we can suppose that they are
deterministic over
transitions producing
priority

2
by the following result of Kuperberg et Skrzypczak
[
37
]
(this property is sometimes called safe determinism).

Lemma 57

(
[
37
]
)
.

Every
history-deterministic

coBüchi automaton
contains an
equivalent

subautomaton
that is
deterministic over

2
-transitions, which can be computed in polynomial time.

Remark 58
.

Two
safe languages
coincide if and only if their restrictions to finite (resp. infinite) words coincide. Indeed, an infinite word
w\in\Sigma^{\omega}
belongs to
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<2}(q)
if and only all its finite prefixes do.

We write
q\mathrel{\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}\leq}_{2}}q^{\prime}
if
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<2}(q)\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<2}(q^{\prime})
; this defines a partial preorder on states of
\mathcal{A}
.
We will sometimes use the term
safe path
to refer to paths in
\mathcal{A}
that do not produce
priority

1
.
The use of the notation “
(<2)
-safe” will be justified by the generalisation of this notion to any
parity automaton
.
The next lemma follows directly from the definition of
safe language
.

A
({<}2)
-safe component
(or just
safe component
) of
\mathcal{A}
is a set of states forming a
strongly connected component
in the
subautomaton
obtained by removing from
\mathcal{A}
all transitions labelled
1
.
By Lemma
57
, we can suppose that these subautomata are
deterministic
.
Also, note that if
\mathcal{A}
is in
normal form
, transitions between different
safe components
produce
priority

1
, that is, states connected by a
safe path
are in the same
safe component
.

Statement of the characterisation of positionality.

We are now ready to state a characterisation of positionality of
prefix-independent

coBüchi recognisable
objectives.

Proposition 60

(Positionality for prefix-independent coBüchi recognisable objectives)
.

A
prefix-independent

coBüchi recognisable
objective is
positional
if and only if it can be
recognised
by a
deterministic

coBüchi automaton
satisfying that within each
safe component
, states are totally ordered by inclusion of
safe languages
.

Before going on with the proof, we discuss two examples.

Example 61
.

In Figure
11
we represent a
coBüchi automaton
over
\Sigma=\{a,b,c\}

recognising
the following objective:

W=\text{ Words containing finitely many factors in }{c(a^{*}cb^{*})^{+}c}.

This is an example of an objective that is not
concave
, as by shuffling words
a(ccaa)^{\omega}\notin W
and
(bbcc)^{\omega}\notin W
we can obtain
(abcc)^{\omega}\in W
. However, we show that it satisfies the hypothesis of Proposition
60
, so it is
positional
. This automaton has a single
safe component
.
The inclusions of the
safe languages
follows from the fact that the transitions are monotone: for every letter
\alpha\in\Sigma
, if
q_{i}\xrightarrow{\alpha:2}q_{j}
and
i\leq i^{\prime}
, then
q_{i^{\prime}}\xrightarrow{\alpha:2}q_{j^{\prime}}
with
j\leq j^{\prime}
.

Figure 11:
Deterministic

coBüchi automaton

recognising
objective
W
from Example
61
.

Example 62
.

Let
\Sigma=\{a,b,c\}
and

W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathtt{Fin}}(ac)\vee{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathtt{Fin}}(bb).

We give a
coBüchi automaton

recognising

W
and satisfying the hypothesis of Proposition
60
in Figure
12
. This automaton has two
safe components
:
S_{1}=\{q_{1},q_{2}\}
and
S_{2}=\{p_{1},p_{2}\}
. The states of each component are totally ordered by inclusion of
safe languages
, as we have
q_{1}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}_{2}}q_{2}
and
p_{1}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}_{2}}p_{2}
.
Therefore,
W
is
positional
.

Figure 12:
Deterministic

coBüchi automaton

recognising
objective
W
from Example
62
. This automaton has two
safe components
:
S_{1}=\{q_{1},q_{2}\}
and
S_{2}=\{p_{1},p_{2}\}
, and the states of each of them are totally ordered by inclusion of
safe languages
.

Remark 63
.

In his PhD thesis
[
34
, Section 6.2]
, Kopczyński introduced a notion of
monotonic automata
over finite words, and showed that if
L\subseteq\Sigma^{*}
is recognised by such an automaton, then the (
prefix-independent
)
objective

\Sigma^{\omega}\setminus L^{\omega}
is
positional

[
34
, Prop 6.6]
.
It turns out that these correspond exactly to the
objectives
characterised in Proposition
60
.

At the level of intuition, starting from a deterministic coBüchi automaton
\mathcal{A}

recognising
a
positional
objective
W
, our proof of the necessity in Proposition
60
proceeds as follows:

•

We turn
\mathcal{A}
into a
history-deterministic

safe centralised
automaton (see definition below) using the minimisation technique of Abu Radi and Kupferman
[
1
]
.

•

Using
positionality
, we prove that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{2}}
defines a total order on each
safe component
.

•

Exploiting the total order, we are able to re-determinise
\mathcal{A}
.

Safe centralisation and safe minimality.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a (possibly
non-deterministic
)
coBüchi automaton
with only one
residual class
.
We say that
\mathcal{A}
is
safe centralised
if, for every pair of states
q_{1},q_{2}
, if
q_{1}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{2}}q_{2}
, then
q_{1}
and
q_{2}
are in the same
safe component
.
We say that
\mathcal{A}
is
safe minimal
if there are no two different states with the same
safe language
.

Lemma 64

(
[
1
]
)
.

Any
prefix-independent

coBüchi recognisable
language can be
recognised
by a
history-deterministic

coBüchi automaton
that is
safe centralised
and
safe minimal
.

Let us present a proof of Lemma
64
.
We say that an automaton is
1
-saturated
if for all pair of states
q,q^{\prime}
, the transition
q\xrightarrow{a:1}q^{\prime}
appears in
\mathcal{A}
.
The
1
-saturation
of a
coBüchi automaton
is the automaton obtained by simply adding all possible transitions of the form
q\xrightarrow{a:1}q^{\prime}
; note that this transformation preserves
determinism over

2
-transitions.

Lemma 65
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a
coBüchi automaton

recognising
a
prefix-independent
language
W
. Then, its
1
-saturation

\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
also recognises
W
. Moreover, if
\mathcal{A}
is
history-deterministic
and
deterministic over

2
-transitions, then so is
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

Proof.

We first show
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})}\subseteq W
.
An
accepting

run over
a word
w
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
eventually only reads transitions with
priority

2
, so it eventually coincides with a run in
\mathcal{A}
. We conclude by
prefix-independence
.
The fact that
W\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})}
and
history-determinism
are clear: one can use the same
resolver
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
as in
\mathcal{A}
.
∎

Total order in each safe component.

The intuitive idea on why having states of a same
safe component
totally ordered by
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{2}}
is necessary for positionality is the same than in the case of
closed objectives
(Lemma
33
): if
q
and
q^{\prime}
are incomparable, there are two words
w,w^{\prime}
that produce
priority

1
from one state but not from the other.
In a game, if
Eve
has not kept track of where we are in the automaton, she will not know what is the best option between
w
and
w^{\prime}
.
However, an issue arises when turning this idea into an actual proof: one needs to build two full differentiating runs from
q
and
q^{\prime}
; producing
priority

1
just once does not suffice.

Safe centrality
will come in handy for this purpose.

By definition, if
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\nleq}_{2}}q^{\prime}
, there is a word which produces
priority

1
when read from
q^{\prime}
, and stays in the corresponding
safe component
when read from
q
.
The following lemma exploits
safe centrality
to extend those runs to synchronise them in the same state, while the run starting from
q
remains safe.
For the purpose of the warm up, we only prove it assuming
\mathcal{A}
is
deterministic
; extending it to the
history-deterministic
case requires some additional technicalities that will be dealt with in Section
5.2
.

Lemma 67

(Total order in each safe component)
.

\mathcal{A}
be a
deterministic

coBüchi automaton

recognising
a

objective

.

.

Thus consider the
game
in which

and

; she can
win

.
∎

Determinisation.

We have stated last two lemmas of the previous paragraph for
deterministic
automata, in order to simplify the presentation.
However,
safe centralisation
only yields
history-deterministic
automata.
We now explain how to use the total order from Lemma
67
to determinise
HD

coBüchi automata

recognising

positional
languages.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a
normalised
,
history-deterministic
and
deterministic over

2
-transitions
coBüchi automaton
recognising a
prefix-independent

positional
language. Order
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{2}}
is total over each
safe component
, by Lemma
67
.
We show how to rearrange the
1
-transitions in order to define an
equivalent

deterministic

automaton

\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
with the same structure of
safe components
.

Let
\{S_{1},S_{2},\dots,S_{k}\}
be the
safe components
of
\mathcal{A}
, enumerated in an arbitrary order.
If a word
w\in\Sigma^{\omega}
is
accepted by

\mathcal{A}
, there is a
run over

w
that eventually stays in one of the components
S_{i}
.
The main idea is that, when reading a word
w
, we can
resolve
the
non-determinism
by trying each
safe component
in a round-robin fashion.
If for a state
q
and for a letter
a\in\Sigma
there is a (unique) transition
q\xrightarrow{a:2}
, we keep it as the only
a
-transition
from
q
.
If there is no transition
q\xrightarrow{a:2}
, and
q
belongs to
S_{i}
, we define a transition
q\xrightarrow{a:1}q^{\prime}
towards some
q^{\prime}
in
S_{i+1}
.
The total order in
S_{i+1}
identifies a state in
S_{i+1}
which is the best to go to: we define
q\xrightarrow{a:1}q_{i+1}^{\max}
, where
q_{i+1}^{\max}
is the unique maximal state of
S_{i+1}
for the total order
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{2}}
.
This defines a
deterministic
automaton
\mathcal{A}
’.

We prove that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}
. Clearly
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})}\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}
, as
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a
subautomaton
of the
1
-saturation
of
\mathcal{A}
.
To show the other inclusion, let
w\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}
. There is a
run over

w
in
\mathcal{A}
that eventually remains in a
safe component
, without loss of generality, we assume that it is
S_{1}
.
Let
w^{\prime}=w_{1}^{\prime}w_{2}^{\prime}\dots
be a suffix of
w
labelling a
run
in
S_{1}
:
q^{1}\xrightarrow{w_{1}^{\prime}}q^{2}\xrightarrow{w_{2}^{\prime}}\dots
. Consider a
run over

w^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.
If this
run
never visits
S_{1}
, it must be because it eventually remains in some
safe component
, so
w^{\prime}
is
accepted by

\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
in that case. If the run eventually arrives to
S_{1}
(at the i
th
step), it will arrive to the maximal element
q_{1}^{\max}
.
At this point, the run in
\mathcal{A}
is in
q^{i}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{2}}q_{1}^{\max}
. Since
w_{i}^{\prime}w_{i+1}^{\prime}\dots\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<2}(q^{i})\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<2}(q_{1}^{\max})
, the run over this suffix is
safe
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
, and word
w
is
accepted by

\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

Example 68
.

The automaton from Figure
12
has the shape we have described: transitions producing
priority

1
cycle between the two
safe components
, and they go to the maximal state of the other component (
p_{1}\xrightarrow{b:1}q_{2}
and
q_{1}\xrightarrow{c:1}p_{2}
).

Generalisation to non prefix-independent coBüchi recognisable languages

To remove the
prefix-independence
assumption, we work with the
localisation to residuals
of the objectives, as defined in Section
4.3
.
If
W
is a
positional
objective, for each residual
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[u]}
the objective
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{[u]}}
is
positional
.
In turns out that this property, together with the hypothesis over residuals that were already necessary for
open objectives
, provides a characterisation.

Proposition 69
.

Let
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
be a
coBüchi recognisable
language. Then,
W
is
positional
if and only if:

•

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is totally ordered,

•

W
is
progress consistent
, and

•

for all
residual class

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[u]}
, objective
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{[u]}}
is
positional
.

This result is not fully satisfying (and hard to prove directly), as it relies on the
positionality
of languages
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{[u]}}
.
As these objectives are
prefix-independent
, we have a characterisation for their
positionality
(Proposition
60
), and we can put them together to obtain a statement using exclusively structural properties of
parity automata
.
The statement we obtain uses a decomposition of parity automata in three layers:

•

States are totally
preordered
by their
residual class
(layer 0).

•

Within each
residual class
, states are grouped into
safe components
(layer 1).

•

Within each
safe component
, states are totally ordered by inclusion of the
safe languages
(layer 2).

This decomposition foreshadows the definition of
structured

signature automata
that we will use in Section
5.2
to derive a characterisation of
positionality
for all
\omega
-regular
languages.

Proposition 70
.

Let
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
be a
coBüchi recognisable
language. Then,
W
is
positional
if and only if:

•

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is totally ordered,

•

W
is
progress consistent
, and

•

W
can be
recognised
by a
deterministic

coBüchi automaton

\mathcal{A}
such that, for all
residual class

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]}
, the
local automaton of the residual

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}}_{[q]}
satisfies that its
safe components
are totally ordered by inclusion of
safe languages
.

We do not include a proof of this proposition; it is a special case of Theorem
23
.

Example 71
.

We consider the following objective over the alphabet
\Sigma=\{a,b,c\}
:

W=\Sigma^{*}a^{\omega}\cup\Sigma^{*}b^{\omega}\cup c\Sigma^{*}c\Sigma^{\omega}.

This objective was studied in
[
4
, Lemma 12]
to show that there are
positional
objectives that are not
concave
, nor
bipositional
(objectives from Examples
50
and
61
also have this property); their proof of
positionality
is quite involved.

A
coBüchi automaton

recognising
objective
W
is depicted in Figure
14
. Its
residuals
are totally ordered, and it is easy to check that it is
progress consistent
.
Moreover, all its
safe components
are trivial. Therefore,
Proposition
70
implies that it is
positional
.

Figure 14:
Automaton
recognising
objective
W
from Example
71
.

4.5
Towards objectives of higher complexity: An example

We revisit the example from Figure
4
, depicted here in Figure
15
. It
recognises
the
objective
of words that either contain ‘
a
’ infinitely often, or contain no ‘
a
’ at all and only finitely many occurrences of the factor ‘
bb
’:

W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathtt{Inf}}(a)\vee({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathtt{No}}(a)\wedge{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathtt{Fin}}(bb)),\;\text{ over }\Sigma=\{a,b,c\}.

This
objective
is neither
Büchi
nor
coBüchi recognisable
, so none of the characterisations of this section applies to it. However, we can combine the techniques presented above to equip
\mathcal{A}
with a “nicely behaved” total order. In the next section, we will see that this can be formalised as the fact that
\mathcal{A}
is a
deterministic

fully progress consistent

signature automaton
, so by Theorem
23
,
W
is
positional
.

Figure 15:
Automaton
recognising
the objective
W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathtt{Inf}}(a)\vee({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathtt{Fin}}(bb)\wedge{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathtt{No}}(a))
.

Objective
W
has two
residuals
:
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\varepsilon}^{-1}W
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}x}^{-1}W
.
It is clear that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}a}^{-1}W\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\varepsilon}^{-1}W
, and, since there is no transition
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[a]}\xrightarrow{}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[\varepsilon]}
, it is trivially
progress consistent
.
The
states associated to

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[a]}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[\varepsilon]}
are, respectively,
\{q_{1}\}
and
\{q_{2},q_{3}\}
.
The
subautomaton
over
\{q_{1}\}

recognises
the
Büchi objective

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Buchi}(a)}
, which is
positional
.
Let us focus on the
subautomaton
induced by
\{q_{2},q_{3}\}
, that coincides with
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}}_{[\varepsilon]}
.
We observe that it satisfies the hypothesis of Lemma
51
: transitions with
priority

0

act uniformly
within
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}}_{[\varepsilon]}
; indeed, these transitions are those reading letter
a
(in red).
Consider the restriction of this subautomaton to letters
\{b,c\}
. The obtained automaton
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}}_{[\varepsilon]}^{\prime}
is a
coBüchi automaton
, satisfying the hypothesis of Lemma
67
: the states of the
safe component
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}}_{[\varepsilon]}^{\prime}
are totally ordered by inclusion of
safe languages
, as
q_{2}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}_{2}}q_{3}
.
In this way, we obtain a decomposition such that:

•

Residuals
are totally ordered by inclusion, and are
progress consistent
.

•

0
-transitions
act uniformly
within the
states of
each
residual class
.

•

The
safe components
of the
coBüchi automata
obtained as the restriction of each class to transitions with
priority

\geq 1
are totally ordered by inclusion of
safe languages
.

Generalising such decomposition to any
parity automaton
will be the central point of the next section.

We also note that the
\varepsilon
-completion
of this automaton presented in Figure
4
follows the decomposition presented here:
\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:0}
-transitions follow the order of the residuals, and
\xrightarrow{2}
-transitions the one given by the inclusion of safe languages.
This procedure of
\varepsilon
-completion
will be generalised in Section
5.3
.

5
Obtaining the structural characterisation of positionality

We now move on to the proof of Theorem
23
.
The first step is to identify the common structural properties of
deterministic

parity automata

recognising

positional
objectives.
In Section
5.1
, we define a class of
parity automata
, which we call
signature
automata, that underscores this structure.
We also introduce
full progress consistency
, a further necessary condition for automata recognising
positional
languages.
To obtain the implication from
(6)
to
(6)
in Theorem
23
we need then to show how to obtain a
fully progress consistent

signature automaton
for a
positional

\omega
-regular
objective.
This is the most technical part of the proof, and it is the object of Section
5.2
.
We then proceed to defining
\varepsilon
-complete automata
and closing the cycle of implications in Section
5.3
.

5.1
Signature automata and full progress consistency

Before finally moving on to the crucial definition of
signature automata
, we need more precise concepts of congruences which we introduce now.

5.1.1
Priority-faithful congruences and quotient automata

Priority-faithful congruences.

We recall that a
congruence
in an automaton allows us to define a
quotient

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\sim$}}\right.}}
, which is a
deterministic

automaton structure
. However, in general, no
colouring with priorities
can be defined
on top of

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\sim$}}\right.}}
in a sensible way, as the
congruence
does not have to be compatible with the
output priorities
of the automaton. We now strengthen the definition of
congruence
for parity automata so that it will be possible to define an approximation of a correct parity condition
on top of
the
quotient automaton
.

Definition 72

(
[0,x]
-faithful congruence)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a
parity automaton
and let
\sim
be a
congruence
over its set of states
Q
. We say that
\sim
is
[0,x]
-faithful
if:

•

for each
0\leq y\leq x
,
y
-transitions

are uniform
over
\sim
-classes and relation
\sim
is a
congruence for
y
-transitions
, and

•

relation
\sim
is a
congruence for
({>}x)
-transitions
.

Stated differently, a relation
\sim
is a
[0,x]
-faithful congruence
if, whenever there is a transition
q\xrightarrow{a:y}p
with
priority

y\leq x
, then for every
q^{\prime}\sim q
a transition
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a}p^{\prime}
produces
priority

y
and goes to a state
p^{\prime}\sim p
.
If there is a transition
q\xrightarrow{a:y}p
producing
priority

y>x
, we only require that transitions
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:>x}p^{\prime}
produce
priorities

>x
and go to
p^{\prime}\sim p
(but the exact
priority
produced may differ). (We remark that, although it is not explicitly imposed,
({>}x)
-transitions

are uniform
over
\sim
-classes by the first property. Also, we recall that we assume that automata are
complete
.)

Remark 73

(
[0,x]
-faithful congruences for deterministic automata)
.

For
deterministic
automata we can give a simpler definition. An equivalence relation
\sim
on a
deterministic automaton

\mathcal{A}
is a
[0,x]
-faithful congruence
if and only if, whenever
q\sim_{x}q^{\prime}
,
q\xrightarrow{a:y}p
and
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:y^{\prime}}p^{\prime}
, then
p\sim p^{\prime}
and
y=y^{\prime}
if
y\leq x
.

Remark 74
.

A
[0,x]
-faithful congruence
is
[0,y]
-faithful
for any
y\leq x
.

({\leq}x)
-quotient automata.

What the definition of
[0,x]
-faithful congruence
tells us is that transitions producing priorities
y\leq x
are well defined in the
quotient automaton

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\sim$}}\right.}}
, in the sense that we can associate a
priority

y
to these transitions reliably. For transitions producing priorities
>x
, on the other hand, we only obtain the information that the
priority
produced from any state of the class will be large, but we lose some precision.

Definition 75

(
({\leq}x)
-quotient automata)
.

If
\sim
is a
[0,x]
-faithful congruence
, we can define the
({\leq}x)
-quotient of
\mathcal{A}
by
\sim
to be the
parity automaton

\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{{\scriptsize$\begin{matrix}[l]\phantom{.}\\[-2.56073pt]
{\sim}\\[-0.56905pt]
\hskip-4.55244pt{{{{{\leq}x}}}}\end{matrix}$}}\right.}}
given by:

•

Its set of states are the
\sim
-classes of
\mathcal{A}
.

•

The initial state is
[q_{\mathsf{init}}]
, where
q_{\mathsf{init}}
is the initial state of
\mathcal{A}
.

•

For
y\leq x
, there is a transition
[q]\xrightarrow{a:y}[p]
if
\mathcal{A}
has a transition
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:y}p^{\prime}
with
q^{\prime}\in[q]
,
p^{\prime}\in[p]
.

•

There is a transition
[q]\xrightarrow{a:x^{\prime}}[p]
if
\mathcal{A}
has a transition
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:>x}p^{\prime}
with
q^{\prime}\in[q]
,
p^{\prime}\in[p]
; where
x^{\prime}=x+1
if
x
even, and
x^{\prime}=x
if
x
odd.

The automaton
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\begin{matrix}[l]\phantom{.}\\[-2.56073pt]
{\sim}\\[-0.56905pt]
\hskip-4.55244pt{{{{{\leq}x}}}}\end{matrix}$}}\right.}}
is defined so transitions coming from those producing a
priority

>x
in
\mathcal{A}
are assigned the least important odd
priority
. This guarantees that the
projection
of
runs
that eventually only produce priorities
>x
in
\mathcal{A}
are
rejecting
in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\begin{matrix}[l]\phantom{.}\\[-2.56073pt]
{\sim}\\[-0.56905pt]
\hskip-4.55244pt{{{{{\leq}x}}}}\end{matrix}$}}\right.}}
. The next lemma refines this comment.

Lemma 76
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a
parity automaton
and let
\sim
be a
[0,x]
-faithful congruence
over it.
The
({\leq}x)
-quotient
of
\mathcal{A}
by
\sim

recognises
the language:

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{{\scriptsize$\begin{matrix}[l]\phantom{.}\\[-2.56073pt]
{\sim}\\[-0.56905pt]
\hskip-4.55244pt{{{{{\leq}x}}}}\end{matrix}$}}\right.}})}=\{w\in\Sigma^{\omega}\mid w\text{ is {\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}accepted with an even priority} }y\leq x\text{ in }\mathcal{A}\}.

Moreover, if
\mathcal{A}
is in
normal form
, then so is
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{{\scriptsize$\begin{matrix}[l]\phantom{.}\\[-2.56073pt]
{\sim}\\[-0.56905pt]
\hskip-4.55244pt{{{{{\leq}x}}}}\end{matrix}$}}\right.}}
.

Proof.

A
run

\rho
in
\mathcal{A}
produces a
priority

y\leq x
infinitely often if and only its
projection
in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\begin{matrix}[l]\phantom{.}\\[-2.56073pt]
{\sim}\\[-0.56905pt]
\hskip-4.55244pt{{{{{\leq}x}}}}\end{matrix}$}}\right.}}
produces
priority

y
infinitely often, which gives the equality of the languages.
It is a direct check that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\begin{matrix}[l]\phantom{.}\\[-2.56073pt]
{\sim}\\[-0.56905pt]
\hskip-4.55244pt{{{{{\leq}x}}}}\end{matrix}$}}\right.}}
inherits being in
normal form
.
∎

5.1.2
Signature automata

We give the definition of
signature automata
, at the core of our characterisation.

We say that a sequence of
total preorders

\leq_{0},\leq_{1},\leq_{2},\dots,\leq_{k}
over
Q
is a
collection of nested total preorders
if
\leq_{i}

refines

\leq_{i-1}
, for
i>1
.
We note that, in that case, the
induced equivalence relation

\sim_{i}
also
refines

\sim_{i-1}
.

Definition 77

(Signature automaton)
.

Let
d\in\mathbb{N}
be a
priority
. A
d
-signature automaton
is a
semantically deterministic

parity automaton

\mathcal{A}

together with a
collection of nested total preorders

\mathrel{\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}\leq}_{0}},\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{1}},\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{2}},\dots,\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{d}}
over
Q
such that:
6
6

6

For notational convenience, we let
\sim_{-2}
be the trivial relation over
\mathcal{A}
throughout this definition. That is,
q\sim_{-2}p
for all pairs of states in
Q
.

I)

Refinements of residual inclusion.
Preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{0}}

refines
the preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}}_{\mathcal{A}}
given by the inclusion of
residuals
.

II)

Faithful partitions at even layers.
For
0\leq x\leq d
,
x
even, the equivalence relation
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
is a
[0,x]
-faithful congruence
.

({<}x)
-safe separation
at odd layers.
For

,
x

:

IV)

Local monotonicity
of
({\geq}x)
-transitions.
For an even
priority

x\leq d
, transitions using priorities
{\geq}x
are
monotone for
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
over each
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}
class. That is, for
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}q^{\prime}
, if
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}q^{\prime}
:

q\xrightarrow{a:\geq x}p\;\;\implies\;\;q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:\geq x}p^{\prime},\;p\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}p^{\prime}\;\text{ and }p\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}p^{\prime},\;\text{ for all }a\text{-transitions from }q^{\prime}.

We say that
\mathcal{A}
is a
signature automaton
if it is a
d
-signature automaton
, for
d
the maximal
priority
appearing in
\mathcal{A}
.

We note that even and odd preorders play a completely different role in the previous definition. In fact, the only purpose of odd preorders is to delimit the areas in which the
local monotonicity
property will apply. Item
(III)
constrains
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}
-classes to be “sufficiently large”.

Remark 78
.

We note that, by Item
(IV)
, for
x
even the equivalence relations
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}
is a
congruence for

{\geq}x
-transitions
. However, the restrictions on these odd preorders are much weaker, as we do not impose them to be
faithful
.

Example 79
.

Consider the automaton
\mathcal{A}
from Figure
15
from the warm-up. This automaton has
3
states,
q_{1},q_{2}
, and
q_{3}
. It can be equipped with the structure of a
signature automaton
as follows:

•

Preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{0}}
is given by the inclusion of residuals:
q_{1}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}_{0}}q_{2},q_{3}
, and
q_{2}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{0}}q_{3}
.

•

Preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{1}}
coincides with preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{0}}
.

•

Preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{2}}
is a total order:
q_{1}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}_{2}}q_{2}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}_{2}}q_{3}
.

Signature automata are not minimal in general, but we conjecture that by merging
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{d}}
-equivalent states we should obtain a minimal automaton (see Section
9.3
for more discussions).

5.1.3
Full progress consistency.

The existence of a
signature automaton

recognising
an objective
W
does not suffice to ensure
positionality
of

.
The problem is similar to the one we encountered when studying
open
objectives in Section
4.2
: there are
open
objectives whose

are totally ordered but their are not
positional
(see Example
36
). In that case, we needed to add the property of
progress consistency
to characterise
positionality
.
We generalise this notion to
signature automata
with multiple preorders.

5.1.4
Structured signature automata from semantic properties of languages

To prove the implication
(6)

\implies

(6)
from Theorem
23
, we build a
signature automaton
from a
deterministic

parity automaton

\mathcal{A}

recognising

recursively.
In order to be able to carry out the recursion, we will in fact obtain a
signature automaton
with even stronger properties. This reinforcement of

is done by ensuring that the preorders
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
come from semantic properties of the automata, for which the notion of
{<}x

will play a major role.
The properties that are imposed are essentially a generalisation of the ones satisfied by the canonical
history-deterministic
coBüchi automata defined by Abu Radi and Kupferman
[

]
.

Remark 83
.

The partition of
\mathcal{A}
into
{<}x
-safe components
is a
refinement
of its partition into
{<}y
-safe components
, for
y\leq x
.

For the following, we fix a
parity automaton

\mathcal{A}
in
normal form
using priorities in
[0,d_{\max}]
. For each
x\in[1,d_{\max}]
, we will totally order the
{<}x
-safe components
of
\mathcal{A}
in such a way that these orders successively refine each other.
For
x\in[1,d_{\max}]
we let
\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}S}^{{<}x}_{1},\dots,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{k_{x}}
be the
{<}x
-safe components
of
\mathcal{A}
.
For
x=1
, we let
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}1}_{1}<_{1}S_{2}^{<1}<_{1}\dots<_{1}S_{k_{1}}^{<1}
be an arbitrary order over the
{<}1
-safe components
.
Assume that an order has already been fixed at level
x-2
. Then, we fix an arbitrary total order for the
{<}x
-safe components
contained in a same
{<}(x-1)
-safe components
, which yields a total order for the set of all those safe components, that refines the previous layers.
From now on, we assume that the enumerations
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{1},\dots,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{k_{x}}
correspond to these orders:
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{i}<_{x}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{j}
if
i<j
.

Structured signature automata.

The
preorders
of the
signature automaton
we plan to build will correspond to the following semantic properties:

1.

Preorder
0
given by inclusion of residuals.
Preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{0}}
corresponds to the inclusion of
residuals
:

q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{0}}p\;\iff\;{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}_{q}})}\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}_{p}})}.

2.

Odd layers correspond to safe components.
For
x\geq 2
even, we define
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x-1}}
by:

q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x-1}}p\;\iff\;{q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}_{x-2}}p}\text{ or }[{q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}p}\text{ and }q\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{i}\text{ and }p\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{j}\text{ with }i\leq j].

In particular,
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}p

{q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}p}

.

3.

Even preorders given by inclusion of safe languages.
For
x\geq 2
,
x
even, we define
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x-1}}
by:

q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}p\;\iff\;{q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}_{x-1}}p}\text{ or }[{q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}p}\text{ and }{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(q)\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p)].

These preorders already ensure some of the properties required to be a
signature automaton
; mainly, the
local monotonicity
of transitions using large priorities (Item
(IV)
), as well as the
congruence for

{\geq}x
-transitions at
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-classes.
Note, however, that it is not clear (and will be an important part of our proof) that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
is total for even
x
.

Given an (even or odd)
priority

d\in\mathbb{N}
, we say that a
parity automaton

\mathcal{A}
in
normal form
together with
nested preorders

\leq_{0},\leq_{1},\dots,\leq_{d}
as above is a
d
-structured signature automaton
if these
preorders
are
total
and moreover:

4.

Strong congruence of
({\leq}x)
-priorities over even classes.
Let
0\leq x\leq d
,
x
even. For every
y\leq x
:

q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}q^{\prime},\;q\xrightarrow{a:y}p\;\text{ and }\;q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:z}p^{\prime}\;\implies\;z=y\;\text{ and }\;p=p^{\prime}.

5.

Classes at layer
x
are
({>}x)
-connected.
For
0\leq x\leq d
and
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}q^{\prime}
, we have:

q\neq q^{\prime}\;\implies\;\text{ there is a path }q\mathrel{\hbox to28.44pt{\vbox to9.97pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 14.21883pt\lower-5.53249pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

6.

Safe centralisation.
Let
2\leq x\leq d
be an even
priority
, and let
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}p
. Then:

q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\nsim}_{x-1}}p\;\implies\;{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(q)\nsubseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p).

We say that
\mathcal{A}
is a
structured signature automaton
if it is a
d
-structured signature automaton
, for
d
the maximal
priority
appearing in
\mathcal{A}
.

Remark 84
.

We draw the reader’s attention to the fact that in Item
4
we do not only require
p\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}p^{\prime}
, but impose
p=p^{\prime}
. This will be necessary to guarantee that the relations
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{y}}
for even priorities
y>x
are also
congruences for

x
-transitions
.

Lemma 85
.

A
deterministic

d
-structured signature automaton
is a
d
-signature automaton
.

Proof.

The fact that
\leq_{0}
refines the inclusion of residuals is ensured by Item
1
.
Also, the
({<}x)
-safe separation
at odd levels (Item
(III)
) is directly implied by the fact that odd layers correspond to safe components (Item
2
).

We now show by induction on
x
that for each
x\leq d
,
x
even,
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
is a
[0,x]
-faithful congruence
.
Consider two states
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}q^{\prime}
, which rewrites as
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}q^{\prime}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(q)={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p)
, and pick a transition
q\xrightarrow{a:y}p
.
There are two cases.

•

If
y\leq x
, then by Item
4
, we have
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:y}p
.

•

If
y>x
, then by monotonicity of safe languages (Lemma
82
), we have
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:\geq x}p^{\prime}
with
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p^{\prime})={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p)
, and by induction,
p^{\prime}\sim_{x-2}p
.
From Item
6
, it follows that
p^{\prime}\sim_{x-1}p
and thus
p^{\prime}\sim_{x}p
, as required.

We conclude that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
is a
[0,x]
-faithful congruence
.

Finally, the
local monotonicity of
({\geq}x)
-transitions
follows from the fact that even preorders correspond to the inclusion of safe languages (Item
3
) and the monotonicity of safe languages (Lemma
82
).
∎

5.2
From positionality to signature automata

This section is devoted to the proof of the implication
(6)

\implies

(6)
in Theorem
23
.
Many of the ideas in this proof have already appeared in the warm-up section.
However further technical issues stem from the fact that we manipulate general
parity automata
.
Details for a number of proofs are relegated to Appendix
A
.

{globalHyp*}

In the whole section,
W
stands for an
objective
that is
positional over
finite,
\varepsilon
-free

Eve-games
.
These hypotheses will not necessarily be recalled in the statements of propositions.

5.2.1
Outline of the induction

Given a
deterministic

parity automaton

recognising
a
positional
objective, we will recursively define the
preorders
and equivalence relations making
\mathcal{A}
a
structured signature automaton
. The base case consists in showing that the preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{0}}
given by the inclusion of residuals is total, and ensuring Item
4
of the definition for this preorder. For the recursion step, we suppose that we have a
deterministic

(x-2)
-structured signature automaton

\mathcal{A}

recognising

W
, for
x
even, and we define preorders
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x-1}}
and
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
over
\mathcal{A}
as imposed by Items
2
and
3
. Then, we apply a sequence of operations, after which we obtain an
equivalent

deterministic

automaton
, that is either
x
-structured signature
, or has strictly less states than
\mathcal{A}
.
In the first case, we continue to define preorders
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x+1}}
and
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x+2}}
; in the second case, we restart the structuration procedure from the beginning, with a strictly smaller automaton. In both cases, we conclude by induction.

We conjecture that we can sequentially obtain all the preorders, without having to restart the construction at each step. However, we have not been able to overcome some technical difficulties preventing us to do so. We refer to the final subsection of Appendix
A
for more details.

We give a more detailed account on the specific operations we apply to obtain the different items of the definition of a
structured signature automaton
and their order:

i)

Relation
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}
and safe centralisation.
We define
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}
, as determined by Item
2
. Applying a generalisation of the procedure from
[
1
]
, we
({<}x)
-safe centralise

\mathcal{A}
, obtaining an equivalent automaton satisfying Item
6
. The resulting automaton is no longer
deterministic
, but it is
history-deterministic
and has a very restricted and controlled amount of
non-determinism
.

ii)

Total order in safe components.
We prove that the states of each
({<}x)
-safe component
are totally ordered by inclusion of
({<}x)
-safe languages
(for which we rely on the
safe centralisation
hypothesis). This shows that the preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
given by the inclusion of
safe languages
(Item
3
) is total.

iii)

Re-determinisation.
We determinise automaton
\mathcal{A}
, while preserving previously obtained properties. For this, the fact that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
is total will be key.

iv)

Uniformity of
x
-transitions.
Finally, we show that either
\mathcal{A}
already satisfies Items
4
and
5
, or we can trim the automaton to an
equivalent
strictly smaller one.

Moreover, we show that all these transformations can be performed in polynomial time.

This establishes that an objective
W
that is
positional over
finite,
\varepsilon
-free

Eve-games
can be
recognised
by a
deterministic

structured signature
automaton.
At the end of the section, we show that such an automaton must be
fully progress consistent
(Lemma
94
).

5.2.2
Constructing structured signature automata for positional languages

Let
\mathcal{A}=(Q,\Sigma,q_{\mathsf{init}},[0,d_{\max}],\Delta,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{parity}})
be a
deterministic

parity automaton

recognising

W
, and suppose that
W
is
positional over
finite,
\varepsilon
-free

Eve-games
.
We assume that
\mathcal{A}
is in
normal form
.

In this subsection, we will apply successive transformations to the automaton
\mathcal{A}
, ensuring an increasing list of properties.
At the beginning of each paragraph, we clearly state the properties that are assumed.
We allow ourselves to omit these hypotheses in the statements of propositions inside the paragraphs.

Base case: Preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{0}}
.

We define
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{0}}p
if
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}_{q}})}\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}_{p}})}
, as imposed by Item
1
.
In Lemma
33
, we showed that
positionality
of
W
implies that this order is total. However, in our proof we used infinite, and not necessarily
\varepsilon
-free
games. It is not difficult to modify the proof to adapt to this set of minimal hypotheses, using
\omega
-regularity
of
W
. We give all details in Appendix
A
(Lemma
151
).
Items
2
,
3
, and
6
are trivially satisfied.
Therefore, it suffices to show that we can obtain an automaton such that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{0}}
is a
strong congruence for transitions
producing
priority

0
(Item
4
), and that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{0}}
-equivalent states can be connected by paths producing priority
{>}x
(Item
5
). For this, we apply exactly the same method presented in Section
4.3
: we obtain a
polished automaton
and show that it satisfies the desired properties. This proof will be covered in the recursive step; the case
x=0
does not present any particularity.

Moving on to the inductive step, for the rest of the subsection, we let
x
be an even priority such that
2<x\leq d_{\max}
and assume that
\mathcal{A}
is a
deterministic

(x-2)
-structured signature automaton
.

Safe centrality and relation
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}
.

We say that an automaton with a
preorder

\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x-2}}
is
({<}x)
-safe centralised
if
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
-equivalent states that are comparable for the inclusion of
({<}x)
-safe languages
are in the same
({<}x)
-safe component
.

Remark 86
.

For automata in
normal form

({<}x)
-safe centrality
can be stated as:
if
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}p
and there is no
({<}x)
-safe path
connecting
q
and
p
, then
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(q)\nsubseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p)
.

Lemma 87

(
({<}x)
-safe centralisation)
.

There exists a
(x-2)
-structured signature
automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}

equivalent to

\mathcal{A}
which is:

•

deterministic over
transitions with
priority
different from
x-1
,

•

homogeneous
,

•

history-deterministic
, and

•

({<}x)
-safe centralised
.

Moreover,
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
can be obtained in polynomial time from
\mathcal{A}
and
|\mathcal{A}^{\prime}|\leq|\mathcal{A}|
.

Lemma
87
.

The proof of this lemma is a refinement of the corresponding result for
coBüchi automata
presented in the warm-up (Lemma
64
): we saturate
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
-classes of the original automaton
\mathcal{A}
with
(x-1)
-transitions
, and then remove
redundant

({<}x)
-safe components
recursively until obtaining a
({<}x)
-safe centralised
automaton. We include all details in Appendix
A
(page
A.2.2
).

Lemma
87
allows us to define
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}
satisfying all required properties:
for
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}p
, we define
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x-1}}p
if and only if
q\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{i}
and
p\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{j}
with
i\leq j
, where
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{i}
are the
({<}x)
-safe components
of
\mathcal{A}
enumerated following the order described in Section
5.1
.
By definition, Item
2
is satisfied, and by
({<}x)
-safe centralisation
of
\mathcal{A}
, so is Item
6
.

Preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
: Total order given by safe languages

In all this paragraph we assume that
\mathcal{A}
is an automaton as obtained in the previous paragraph, that is: it has
nested preorders
defined up to
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x-1}}
making it a
(x-2)
-structured signature automaton
and satisfying Items
2
and
6
for relation
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}
. Moreover, it is
history-deterministic
,
homogeneous
, and the only non-determinism of
\mathcal{A}
appears in
(x-1)
-transitions
.

We define
preorder

\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
as imposed by Item
3
:

q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}p\;\iff q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}_{x-1}}p\text{ or }[q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}p\text{ and }\;{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(q)\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p)],

and recall that it follows that
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}p
if and only if
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}p
and there is a
(<x)
-safe path
from
q
to
p
.

Remark 88
.

Using Item
4
for priorities
y\leq x-2
and Lemma
82
for transitions with priority
\geq x
, we get that
relation
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
is a
congruence for
transitions with a priority different from
x-1
.
Moreover, over each
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}
-class, transitions with priority
{\geq}x
are
monotone for

\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
.

Our objective is now to show that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
is
total
over each
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}
-class. The proof of this statement uses the same ideas as the corresponding result from the warm-up (Lemma
67
). In particular, the main technical point resides in proving that, for two states
q_{1}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\nleq}_{x}}q_{2}
, we can force to produce priority
x-1
from
q_{1}
while remaining
{<}x
-safe
from
q_{2}
, and then resynchronise both paths in a same
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-class. This result, stated in Lemma
90
, is the analogue to Lemma
66
from the warm-up. For its proof we strongly rely on the
({<}x)
-safe centralisation
of
\mathcal{A}
and the fine control of its non-determinism.

In the proofs of Lemmas
90
and
91
we will reason at the level of
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-classes. As we only suppose that
\mathcal{A}
is
(x-2)
-structured
, we do not have the
uniformity
of
x
-transitions over
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-classes yet. Lemma
89
below provides a weaker version of this uniformity that will suffice for the arguments in the upcoming lemmas.

Lemma 89

(Existence of uniform words)
.

Let
p
and
q
be two states from the same
({<}x)
-safe component
.
There is a word
w\in\Sigma^{*}

producing priority
x
uniformly
in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}

leading to

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[p]_{x}}
.

We next state the result that allows us to synchronise runs in a same
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-class.
Its proof is analogous to that of Lemma
66
and can be found in Appendix
A
.

We let
\mathsf{r}
be a
sound resolver
for
\mathcal{A}
, and assume that all states can be reached by a
run induced by
this
resolver
.

(Total order in

Re-obtaining determinism

In this paragraph we assume that
\mathcal{A}
is a
parity automaton

recognising

W
equipped with
nested total preorders
defined up to
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
with all properties obtained until now:

•

it is a
(x-2)
-structured signature automaton
,

•

preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x-1}}
satisfies properties from Items
2
and
6
from the definition of a
structured signature automaton
,

•

preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
satisfies the property from Item
3
from the definition of a
structured signature automaton
,

•

it is
deterministic over
transitions with priorities different from
x-1
,

•

it is
homogeneous
, and

•

it is
history-deterministic
.

We claim that we can obtain a
deterministic

equivalent

automaton
preserving the entire structure of
total preorders
. Moreover, in the obtained automaton we guarantee that relation
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
satisfies Item
4
from the definition of a
structured signature automaton
for priorities
y<x
.

Lemma 92

(Re-determinisation)
.

There is a
deterministic

parity automaton

\mathcal{A}^{\prime}

equivalent to

\mathcal{A}
with
nested total preorders
defined up to
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
satisfying that:

•

it is a
(x-2)
-structured signature automaton
,

•

preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x-1}}
satisfies properties from Items
2
and
6
from the definition of a
structured signature automaton
, and

•

preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
is a
congruence
and satisfies the property from Item
3
and, for priorities
y<x
, also that from Item
4
.

Moreover, automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
can be computed in polynomial time from
\mathcal{A}
and
|\mathcal{A}^{\prime}|\leq|\mathcal{A}|
.

The idea of the proof is a direct generalisation of the one presented in the warm-up for
coBüchi automata
(page
4.4
): we redefine the
(x-1)
-transitions of the automaton in such a way that we ensure that a run that changes of
{<}x
-safe component
infinitely often passes through all these components in a round-robin fashion. The total order
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
allows us to identify a maximal state in each component, so we can make a deterministic choice.
Formal details can be found in Appendix
A
(page
A.2.4
).

Uniformity of
x
-transitions over
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-classes

We assume that
\mathcal{A}
is a
deterministic

parity automaton

recognising

W
with
nested total preorders
defined up to
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
satisfying all conditions stated in Lemma
92
.
The objective of this paragraph is to obtain the remaining properties of a
x
-structured signature automaton
(Items
4

and
5
).

Lemma 93

(Uniformity of
x
-transitions over
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-classes)
.

There is a
deterministic

parity automaton

\mathcal{A}^{\prime}

equivalent to

\mathcal{A}
such that either:

•

\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is an
x
-structured signature automaton
with
|\mathcal{A}^{\prime}|\leq|\mathcal{A}|
, or

•

|\mathcal{A}^{\prime}|<|\mathcal{A}|
.

In both cases, such an automaton can be computed in polynomial time from
\mathcal{A}
.

The proof of this lemma generalises the techniques introduced in Section
4.3
of the warm-up. Details can be found in Appendix
A
(from page
A.2.5
).
We introduce the
local automaton of a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-class

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
: the automaton originated by keeping the states of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
and paths connecting them producing priorities
\geq x
.
Using
positionality
and ideas analogous to those from Lemma
45
, we show that these
local automata
admit a well-defined set of
super letters
, that is, there are letters that, if read infinitely often in such a
local automaton
, must produce an
accepting word
.
These letters are exactly the ones carrying priority
x
when read from
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
in the final automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

To obtain the uniformity of
x
-transitions, we might need to simplify the automaton: we introduce
x
-polished automata
, the target form of automata that will allow us to obtain
uniformity
of
x
-transitions.
Using the existence of
super letters
, we show that we can
polish
automaton
\mathcal{A}
by removing
redundant
parts of it.
This operation might break the
normal form
of automaton
\mathcal{A}
,
8
8

8

In fact, we believe that the
polishing operation
does preserve
normality
, but we have not been able to prove it.
but this is not a problem, since in any case it strictly decreases the number of states of the automaton, as desired.

This ends the induction step of the proof, establishing existence of a
deterministic

structured signature
automaton
recognising

W
.

(6)

5.3
From signature automata to positionality through

-complete automata

We now complete the proof of Theorem
23
by showing the two implications
(6)

\implies

(6)
and
(6)

\implies

(6)
.
The implication
(6)

\implies

(6)
follows from Proposition
4
(taken from
[
44
]
) and
(6)

\implies

(6)
is trivial.

5.3.1
\varepsilon
-complete automata

We start with our crucial definition.

Definition 95
.

An
\varepsilon
-complete
automaton
\mathcal{A}
is a
non-deterministic

parity automaton
(with
\varepsilon
-transitions
) with priorities ranging between 0 and
d+1
, where
d
is even, such that

•

the relations
\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:1},\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:3},\dots,\xrightarrow{\varepsilon,d+1}
all define total preorders, each refining the previous one;

•

for each even
x\in\{0,2,\dots,d\}
, the relation
\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x}
is the strict variant of
\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x+1}
: for any
q,q^{\prime}
, it holds that
q\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x}q^{\prime}
if and only if
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x+1}q
does not hold.

We say that an automaton
\mathcal{A}
(which will usually be taken deterministic) is
\varepsilon
-completable
, if one may add
\varepsilon
-transitions to
\mathcal{A}
so as to make it
\varepsilon
-complete
, without augmenting the language.
We say that the resulting (generally non-deterministic) automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is an
\varepsilon
-completion
of
\mathcal{A}
; note that if
\mathcal{A}
is deterministic, then
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is
history-deterministic
(it is even determinisable by pruning).
We refer to Figure
4
in Section
3
for an example.

5.3.2
From signature automata to
\varepsilon
-completable automata

We now prove the implication
(6)

\implies

(6)
from Theorem
23
, which can be stated as follows.

Lemma 96

(From
(6)
to
(6)
in Theorem
23
)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a
fully progress consistent

deterministic

signature automaton
.
Then
\mathcal{A}
is
\varepsilon
-completable
.

We prove Lemma
96
. We refer to the discussion at the end of Section
4.5
(Figure
15
) for an example on the ideas of this proof.
Let
\mathcal{A}
be a
fully progress consistent

deterministic

signature
automaton with
nested preorders

\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{0}},\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{1}},\dots,\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{d}}
and let
W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}
.
Consider the automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
obtained from
\mathcal{A}
by adding, for all even priorities
x\in[0,d]
, transitions
q\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x+1}q^{\prime}
whenever
q^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}q
and
q\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x}q^{\prime}
whenever
q^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}_{x}}q
.
Note that
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
(potentially) has transitions with priorities up to
d+1
.

Remark 97
.

Note that, for
x
even,
q\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:\geq x}p
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
entails
p\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}q
.

Since by definition,
q^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}_{x}}q
is the negation of
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}q^{\prime}
, it follows immediately that
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is
\varepsilon
-complete
. Moreover, as
\mathcal{A}
is a
subautomaton
of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
, the inclusion
W\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})}
is trivial. The difficulty lies in showing that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})}\subseteq W
.

c)

We have that

.

Proof.

In the two first cases we deal with the case of a letter and conclude by induction.

a)

There are two possibilities, depending on whether the letter is
\varepsilon
or not.

•

Transition
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:\geq x}p^{\prime}
with
a\in\Sigma
.
Then
[0,x]
-faithfulness
of
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
gives
p\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}p^{\prime}
and
q\xrightarrow{a:\geq x}p
.
Moreover if
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:x}p^{\prime}
, then by
[0,x]
-faithfulness
,
q\xrightarrow{a:x}p
.

•

Transition
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:\geq x}p^{\prime}
.
Then
p^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}q^{\prime}
and since there is no
x
-jump
,
p^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}q^{\prime}
. Thus
p=q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}q^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}p^{\prime}
.

b)

We distinguish the two same cases.

•

Transition
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:\geq x}p^{\prime}
with
a\in\Sigma
.
Then

({\geq}x)

in
\mathcal{A}
yields

with

78
,
p^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}p
.

•

Transition
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:\geq x}p^{\prime}
.
This implies
p^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}q^{\prime}
and since there is no
(x-1)
-jump

p^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}q^{\prime}
.
Thus we conclude that

and
p=q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}q^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}p^{\prime}
.

Proof of Lemma
96
.

As mentioned above, the inclusion
W\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})}
is trivial, as
\mathcal{A}
is a subautomaton of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
. This shows that, if the converse inclusion holds,
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is determinisable by pruning and therefore it is also
history-deterministic
.

We show
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})}\subseteq W
