5.3.3
Universal graphs from
\varepsilon
-complete automata

We now move on to implication
(6)

\implies

(6)
in Theorem
23
.
We even prove a stronger result:
history-determinism
is sufficient here.

Proposition 101

(Implies
(6)

\implies

(6)
in Theorem
23
)
.

If there is a
\varepsilon
-complete

history-deterministic
automaton
recognising

W
, then there is a
well-ordered

monotone

(\kappa,W)
-universal
graph for each cardinal
\kappa
.

For the rest of the section, we let
\mathcal{A}
be an
\varepsilon
-complete

history-deterministic
automaton
recognising

W
, and we let
d
be even such that
\mathcal{A}
has priorities up to
d+1
, as in the above section.

Closure of an
\varepsilon
-complete automaton

We define the order
\mathrel{\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}\preccurlyeq}}
over
priorities
in
[0,d+1]
that sets
y\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}x
if
x
is “preferable” to
y
, that is:
1\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}3\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}\dots\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}d+1\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}d\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}\dots\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}2\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}0
.

Remark 102
.

For any pair of infinite words
w,w^{\prime}\in[0,d+1]^{\omega}
satisfying that for all
i

w_{i}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}w^{\prime}_{i}
, it holds that:

w\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{parity}}_{[0,d+1]}\implies w^{\prime}\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{parity}}_{[0,d+1]}.

We say that an automaton
\mathcal{A}
is
priority-closed
if:

•

for any states
q,q^{\prime}
, priorities
y^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}y
, and
a\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}

q\xrightarrow{a:y}q^{\prime}\implies q\xrightarrow{a:y^{\prime}}q^{\prime}

•

for any states
p,p^{\prime},q,q^{\prime}
and
a\in\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}
,

p\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:y_{1}}q\xrightarrow{a:y_{2}}q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:y_{3}}p^{\prime}\implies p\xrightarrow{a:\min_{\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}}(y_{1},y_{2},y_{3})}p^{\prime}.

It is easy to turn any automaton into a
priority-closed
one.

Lemma 103
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be an automaton recognising
W
.
There is an automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
recognising
W
which is
priority-closed
.
Moreover, if
\mathcal{A}
is
history-deterministic
and
\varepsilon
-complete
, then so is
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

Proof.

Let
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be obtained by adding to
\mathcal{A}
all transitions of the form
q\xrightarrow{a:y^{\prime}}q^{\prime}
, when
q\xrightarrow{a:y}q^{\prime}
is a transition in
\mathcal{A}
and
y^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}y
, and all transitions of the form
p\xrightarrow{a:\min_{\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}}(y_{1},y_{2},y_{3})}p^{\prime}
, whenever a path
p\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:y_{1}}q\xrightarrow{a:y_{2}}q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:y_{3}}p^{\prime}
appears in
\mathcal{A}
.
Clearly,
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is
priority-closed
,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})}
and if
\mathcal{A}
is
\varepsilon
-complete
, then so is
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.
The fact that this operation preserves
history-determinism
is also clear, once the equality of languages is obtained.
To prove that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})}\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}
, take an accepting
run over

w\in\Sigma^{\omega}
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
. We build a run over
w
in
\mathcal{A}
by replacing any newly added transition
q\xrightarrow{a:y^{\prime}}q^{\prime}
by
q\xrightarrow{a:y}q^{\prime}
, and
p\xrightarrow{a:\min_{\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}}(y_{1},y_{2},y_{3})}p^{\prime}
by
p\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:y_{1}}q\xrightarrow{a:y_{2}}q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:y_{3}}p^{\prime}
, respectively. By Remark
102
, the obtained run is
accepting
in
\mathcal{A}
.
∎

In a
priority-closed
automaton, for each
priority

y
, transitions
\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:y}
define a transitive relation.
If the automaton is moreover
\varepsilon
-complete
, then for each even priority
x
, transitions of the form
\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x+1}
define
total preorders
.

We define
q\mathrel{\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}\geq}_{x}}q^{\prime}
if
q\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x+1}q^{\prime}
.
Note that, since
\mathcal{A}
is
priority-closed
, these preorders are
nested
:
q\geq_{x+2}q^{\prime}
implies
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\geq}_{x}}q^{\prime}
.
Moreover, since
\mathcal{A}
is
\varepsilon
-complete
, for any even
x
:

q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}>}_{x}}q^{\prime}\implies q\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x}q^{\prime}.

Finally, observe that, by
priority-closure
, states
q,q^{\prime}
that are
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{d}}
-equivalent have exactly the same incoming and outgoing transitions, and can thus be merged without altering the language (this transformation preserves
history-determinism
).
Therefore, we may assume that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{d}}
is antisymmetric and thus defines a total order on
Q
.

We write
\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}[q]_{x}}
to denote the equivalence class of
q
associated to preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
. That is,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
contains the states
q^{\prime}
such that
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}q^{\prime}
and
q^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}q
.

Definition of the graph

For the remainder of the section, we fix a cardinal
\kappa
.
Let us first recall the construction of the
(\kappa,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{parity}})
-universal
graph
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\hskip-2.41849pt\mathsf{parity}}
for the
parity objective
over
\{0,\dots,d+1\}
(see Example
6
for a proof of universality). Its vertices are of the form
(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{3},\dots,\lambda_{d+1})\in\kappa^{d/2+1}
, ordered lexicographically, and its edges are given by

(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{d+1})\xrightarrow{x}(\lambda^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime}_{d+1})\iff\begin{cases}(\lambda^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime}_{x-1})\leq(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{x-1}),&\text{ if }x\text{ is even},\\
(\lambda^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime}_{x})<(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{x}),&\text{ otherwise}.\end{cases}

Fix a
priority-closed

\varepsilon
-complete
and
history-deterministic
automaton
\mathcal{A}
with states
Q
such that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{d}}
defines a total order on
Q
.

We define a
\Sigma
-graph

\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
as follows.
Vertices of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
are the tuples
v=(q,\lambda_{1},\lambda_{3},\dots,\lambda_{d+1})\in Q\times\kappa^{d/2+1}
.
We associate to each such vertex the
extended tuple

\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}{\mathsf{ext}}}(v)=({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{0}},\lambda_{1},{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{2}},\lambda_{3},\dots,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{d-1}},\lambda_{d+1}).

We use it to define the total order:
v\leq v^{\prime}
if
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\mathsf{ext}}}(v)
is smaller than
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\mathsf{ext}}}(v^{\prime})
for the lexicographic order.
This is therefore a well-order.
Edges in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
are given by:

(q,\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{d+1})\xrightarrow{a}(q^{\prime},\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{d+1})\;\iff\;\exists y\,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}q\xrightarrow{a:y}q^{\prime}\text{ in }\mathcal{A},\;\;\text{ and }\\[5.69054pt]
(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{d+1})\xrightarrow{y}(\lambda^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda_{d+1})\text{ in }{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\hskip-2.41849pt\mathsf{parity}}.\end{array}\right.

Paths in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
are well-behaved with respect to
W
, as stated below.

Lemma 104
.

Let
(q,\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{d+1})\mathrel{\hbox to15.61pt{\vbox to8.42pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 7.80336pt\lower-4.7597pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

be an infinite path in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
. Then,

.

Proof.

Consider a path

(q^{0},\lambda_{1}^{0},\dots,\lambda_{d+1}^{0})\xrightarrow{w_{0}}(q^{1},\lambda_{1}^{1},\dots,\lambda_{d+1}^{1})\xrightarrow{w_{1}}\dots\text{ in }{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}.

By definition, there are priorities
y_{0},y_{1},\dots
such that

q^{0}\xrightarrow{w_{0}:y_{0}}q^{1}\xrightarrow{w_{1}:y_{1}}\dots\text{ in }\mathcal{A},\;\text{ and }\;\;(\lambda_{1}^{0},\dots,\lambda_{d+1}^{0})\xrightarrow{y_{0}}(\lambda_{1}^{1},\dots,\lambda_{d+1}^{1})\xrightarrow{y_{1}}\dots\text{ in }{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\hskip-2.41849pt\mathsf{parity}}.

Since vertices in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\hskip-2.41849pt\mathsf{parity}}
satisfy the parity objective,
\liminf(y_{0}y_{1}\dots)
is even, thus the above run in
\mathcal{A}
is accepting, and so
w_{0}w_{1}\dots\in(q^{0})^{-1}W
.
∎

Monotonicity

Monotonicity
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
follows from the structural assumptions over
\mathcal{A}
.

Lemma 105
.

The graph
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
is
monotone
.

Proof.

Let

(q,\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{d+1})\xrightarrow{a}(q^{\prime},\lambda^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime}_{d+1})>(q^{\prime\prime},\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{d+1})\text{ in }{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}.

We aim to prove that
(q,\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{d+1})\xrightarrow{a}(q^{\prime\prime},\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{d+1})\text{ in }{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
.
By definition of the transitions of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
, there is a priority
y
such that
q\xrightarrow{a:y}q^{\prime}\text{ in }\mathcal{A}
and
(\lambda_{0},\dots,\lambda_{d+1})\xrightarrow{y}(\lambda^{\prime}_{0},\dots,\lambda^{\prime}_{d+1})\text{ in }{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\hskip-2.41849pt\mathsf{parity}}
.
We remark that, by definition of the order in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
, we have that
({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime\prime}]_{0}},\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{y-1},{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime\prime}]_{y}})\leq({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime}]_{0}},\lambda^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime}_{y-1},{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime}]_{y}})
(for
y
even, similar if
y
odd).
We distinguish four cases:

•

If
y
is even and
({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime}]_{0}},\lambda^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime}_{y-1},{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime}]_{y}})=({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime\prime}]_{0}},\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{y-1},{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime\prime}]_{y}})
.
Then in
\mathcal{A}
,
q\xrightarrow{a:y}q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:y+1}q^{\prime\prime}
thus
q\xrightarrow{a:y}q^{\prime\prime}
, and in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
,
(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{y-1})\geq(\lambda^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime}_{y-1})=(\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{y-1})
, which concludes.

•

If
y
is odd and
({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime}]_{0}},\lambda^{\prime}_{1},\dots,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime}]_{y-1}},\lambda^{\prime}_{y})=({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime\prime}]_{0}},\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{1},\dots,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime\prime}]_{y-1}},\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{y})
.
Then, in
\mathcal{A}
,
q\xrightarrow{a:y}q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:y}q^{\prime\prime}
thus
q\xrightarrow{a:y}q^{\prime\prime}
, and in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
,
(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{y})>(\lambda^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime}_{y})=(\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{y})
which concludes.

•

If for some even
x\leq y
it holds that
({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime}]_{0}},\lambda^{\prime}_{1},{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime}]_{2}},\dots,\lambda^{\prime}_{x-1})=({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime\prime}]_{0}},\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{1},{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime}]_{2}},\dots,\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{x-1})
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime\prime}]_{x}}<{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime}]_{x}}
.
Then in
\mathcal{A}
,
q\xrightarrow{a:y}q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x}q^{\prime\prime}
thus
q\xrightarrow{a:x}q^{\prime\prime}
and in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
,
(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{x-1})\geq(\lambda^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime}_{x-1})=(\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{x-1})
thus
(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{d+1})\xrightarrow{x}(\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{d+1})
which concludes.

•

If for some even
x<y
it holds that
({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime}]_{0}},\lambda^{\prime}_{1},\dots,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime}]_{x}})=({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime\prime}]_{0}},\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{1},\dots,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q^{\prime\prime}]_{x}})
and
\lambda^{\prime}_{x+1}>\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{x+1}
.
Then, in
\mathcal{A}
,
q\xrightarrow{a:y}q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x+1}q^{\prime\prime}
thus
q\xrightarrow{a:x+1}q^{\prime\prime}
and in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
,
(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{x+1})\geq(\lambda^{\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime}_{x+1})>(\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{x+1})
thus
(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{d+1})\xrightarrow{x+1}(\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{1},\dots,\lambda^{\prime\prime}_{d+1})
which concludes.

The other implication
v>v^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a}v^{\prime\prime}\implies v\xrightarrow{a}v^{\prime\prime}
in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
follows exactly the same lines.
∎

Universality of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}

To prove Proposition
101
, there remains to establish
universality
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
, which follows easily from
history-determinism
of
\mathcal{A}
and
universality
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\hskip-2.41849pt\mathsf{parity}}
.

Lemma 106
.

The graph
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}^{\top}}
is
(\kappa,W)
-universal
.

Proof.

We show
universality for trees
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
and conclude by Lemma
5
.
Let
T
be a
\Sigma
-tree
of size
<\kappa
that
satisfies

W
.
Let
\mathsf{r}
be a
sound resolver
for
\mathcal{A}
. We define in a top-down fashion a labelling
\mathsf{r}_{T}:T\to Q
such that, if
w_{1}w_{2}\dots w_{k}
is the labelling of the path from the
root
to a vertex
t
, then
\mathsf{r}_{T}(t)
is the target state of the
run induced by

\mathsf{r}
in
\mathcal{A}
.
In particular,
t\xrightarrow{a}t^{\prime}\text{ in }T
implies that
\mathsf{r}_{T}(t)\xrightarrow{a:x}\mathsf{r}_{T}(t^{\prime})\text{ in }\mathcal{A}
for some priority
x
, and, on each infinite branch
t_{0}\xrightarrow{a_{0}}t_{1}\xrightarrow{a_{1}}\dots
, the
run

\mathsf{r}_{T}(t_{0})\xrightarrow{a_{0}:x_{0}}\mathsf{r}_{T}(t_{1})\xrightarrow{a_{1}:x_{1}}\dots
is
accepting
in
\mathcal{A}
. Stated differently, the
[0,d+1]
-tree

\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}T_{\mathsf{parity}}}
obtained from
T
by replacing each edge
t\xrightarrow{a}t^{\prime}
with the corresponding edge
t\xrightarrow{x}t^{\prime}
such that
\mathsf{r}_{T}(t)\xrightarrow{a:x}\mathsf{r}_{T}(t^{\prime})
,
satisfies
the
parity objective
.

By
(\kappa,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{parity}})
-universality
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\hskip-2.41849pt\mathsf{parity}}
, there exists a
morphism

\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}\phi_{\mathsf{parity}}}:{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}T_{\mathsf{parity}}}\to{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\hskip-2.41849pt\mathsf{parity}}
.
As
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}T_{\mathsf{parity}}}
has the same set of vertices than
T
,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\phi_{\mathsf{parity}}}
defines a mapping from
T
to
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\hskip-2.41849pt\mathsf{parity}}
.
We consider the product mapping
\phi=\mathsf{r}_{T}\times{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\phi_{\mathsf{parity}}}\colon T\to{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
that sends
t\mapsto(\mathsf{r}_{T}(t),{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\phi_{\mathsf{parity}}}(t))
.
It defines a
morphism
, as for any edge
t\xrightarrow{a}t^{\prime}
in
T
it holds that, for some
x
,
\mathsf{r}_{T}(t)\xrightarrow{a:x}\mathsf{r}_{T}(t^{\prime})\text{ in }\mathcal{A}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\phi_{\mathsf{parity}}}(t)\xrightarrow{x}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\phi_{\mathsf{parity}}}(t^{\prime})\text{ in }{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}U}_{\!\mathcal{A}}
.
∎

This completes the proofs of the implications
(6)

\implies

(6)

\implies

(6)
from Theorem
23
, providing a characterisation of
positionality
for
\omega
-regular languages.

6
Two decision procedures

We now establish decidability of
positionality
of
\omega
-regular languages
in polynomial time, stated as Theorem
25
.
We propose two decision procedures.

The first one follows our proof of Theorem
23
and attempts to build a
deterministic

signature
automaton from a given deterministic parity automaton.
We believe that the techniques used in such a procedure may prove interesting also in other contexts (see conclusion in Section
9.3
).

The second procedure is simpler to describe: we give a direct proof that any (non-deterministic) automata recognising a
positional
language is
\varepsilon
-completable
.
However, the proof itself relies on Theorem
23
, and more specifically its consequence Theorem
27
about the closure under union.

6.1
Procedure 1: Recursive decomposition

The first decision procedure we present consists in, given a
deterministic

parity automaton

\mathcal{A}
, applying the construction from Section
5.2
to decide whether
W=\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})
is
positional
.
The general idea is simply to go through that construction, either ending up with a failure indicating that
W
is not positional, or with a
deterministic

structured signature automaton
.
If such an automaton is successfully obtained, it suffices to check
full progress consistency
, which can be done in polynomial time, as explained below.

Complexity of building a signature automata

Most proofs have been already given in Section
5.2
; we also require the following easy lemma.

Lemma 107
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a
parity automaton
and
x
a priority. Assume that
\mathcal{A}
is
deterministic over

{\geq}x
-transitions. Given two states
q,p
in
\mathcal{A}
, we can decide in polynomial time whether
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(q)\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p)
.

We now detail the polynomial-time procedure.
Let
\mathcal{A}
be a
deterministic

parity automaton

recognising

W
.

•

First, we check for each pair of states
q,p
whether
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}_{q}})}\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}_{p}})}
, or
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}_{p}})}\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}_{q}})}
. If for some pair of states these languages are incomparable, then
residuals
of
W
are not totally ordered, and we can conclude that
W
is not
positional
.

Suppose that we have defined total preorders up to
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x-2}}
making
\mathcal{A}
a
(x-2)
-structured signature
automaton.

•

We
{<}x
-safe centralise

\mathcal{A}
, which can be done in polynomial time by Lemma
87
.
The obtained automaton is
deterministic over

{\geq}x
-transitions.

•

We compute the
{<}x
-safe components
of
\mathcal{A}
, which can be done by doing a decomposition in
SCCs
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\left.\kern-1.2pt\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\vphantom{\big|}}{}{}{}\right|_{{\geq}x}}}
.
We check whether, for each
{<}x
-safe component

S
and state
q
, the states in
S\cap{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x-2}}
are
totally preordered
by inclusion of
{<}x
-safe languages
, which can be done in polynomial time by Lemma
107
.
If this is not the case, we conclude that
W
is not
positional
.

•

We remove the non-determinism from
\mathcal{A}
– in polynomial time and without increasing the number of states – by applying Lemma
92
.

•

We compute (in polynomial time) the automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
given by Lemma
93
(see last subsection of Appendix
A
for details).
We check whether
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})}=W
, which can be done in polynomial time (testing equivalence of
deterministic

parity automata

[
23
]
).
If this is not the case, we conclude that
W
is not
positional
.

After these operations, if we have not yet found that
W
is not
positional
, we obtain an
equivalent

deterministic
automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
that is either
x
-structured signature
, or strictly smaller than
\mathcal{A}
.
10
10

10

As mentioned before, we conjecture that the obtained automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is always
x
-structured signature
.
In the former case, we continue defining preorders
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x+1}}
and
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x+2}}
; in the latter, we restart from the beginning.
In total, we repeat at most
d\cdot|Q|
times a sequence of operations that take polynomial time.

Checking full progress consistency

Assume that we have a
deterministic

structured signature automaton

recognising

\mathcal{A}
. We cannot yet conclude that
W
is
positional
, as we do not know whether
\mathcal{A}
is
fully progress consistent

94

W
is
positional
this must be the case. By Theorem
23
, this condition is also sufficient.
We show now that we can check
full progress consistency
of
\mathcal{A}
in polynomial time, finishing the proof of Theorem
25
. For this, we generalise the method from
[
9
, Lemma 25]
.

Lemma 108
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a deterministic

The proof crucially relies on the following lemma.

By Lemma
109
,
\mathcal{A}
is
fully progress consistent
if and only if, for each even priority
x\in[0,d]
and each pair of states
q,p\in Q
such that
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}_{x}}p
:

L_{q\xrightarrow{}p}^{\geq x}\;\bigcap\;\big(\bigcup_{y\text{ odd}}L_{p\xrightarrow{}p}^{y}\big)=\emptyset.

We show that for all pair of states, languages
L_{q\xrightarrow{}p}^{\geq x}
and
L_{q\xrightarrow{}p}^{x}
are regular and we can obtain deterministic finite automata for them in polynomial time.
This implies that we can check the emptiness of intersections above in polynomial time, concluding the proof.

For
L_{q\xrightarrow{}p}^{\geq x}
the previous claim is clear: the finite automaton obtained by taking the
automaton structure
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\left.\kern-1.2pt\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\vphantom{\big|}}{}{}{}\right|_{{\geq}x}}}
and taking
q
and
p
as initial and final states, respectively, is a finite automaton recognising
L_{q\xrightarrow{}p}^{\geq x}
.

For
L_{q\xrightarrow{}p}^{x}
, we consider the automaton over finite words that has as states
(Q\times[0,d])\cup\{(q,{\mathsf{init}})\}
, and
(q,{\mathsf{init}})
and
(p,x)
as initial and final states, respectively.
Transitions of the automaton are of the form
(q_{1},x_{1})\xrightarrow{a}(q_{2},x_{2})
if the transition
q_{1}\xrightarrow{a:y}q_{2}
in
\mathcal{A}
is such that
x_{2}=\min\{x_{1},y\}
.
In words, this automaton keeps track of the run in
\mathcal{A}
from
q
and of the minimal priority produced in the way. It accepts a word if it arrives to
p
while producing as minimal priority
x
, as we wanted.
∎

6.2
Procedure 2:
\varepsilon
-completion

We now prove the following result.

Theorem 110
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a
non-deterministic

parity automaton
recognising a
positional
language
W
.
Then for each pair of states
q,q^{\prime}\in Q
, and for each even priority
x
, one may add (at least) one of the transitions

q\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x}q^{\prime}\qquad\text{ or }\qquad q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x+1}q

without augmenting the language of
\mathcal{A}
.

Before proving Theorem
110
, we argue that decidability of
positionality
in polynomial time (Theorem
25
) follows.
Let
\mathcal{A}_{0}
be a
deterministic

parity automaton
recognising a language
W
and using
d
as maximal
priority
(assumed even).
We build an
\varepsilon
-completion
of
\mathcal{A}_{0}
as follows.
At each step, pick a pair of states
(q,q^{\prime})
such that neither
q\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x}q^{\prime}
nor
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x+1}q
belongs to the current automaton, for
x\leq d
even.
Then try to add one of these transitions, and see if the language increases (checking whether
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}\subseteq W
can be done in polynomial time since
W
is
recognised
by the
deterministic
automaton
\mathcal{A}_{0}

[
23
]
).
If the language does not increase for one of the two transitions, then proceed to the next step; otherwise conclude that
W
is not
positional
thanks to Theorem
110
.

After polynomially-many steps, we obtain an automaton such that for each pair of states
(q,q^{\prime})
and for each even
x
, either
q\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x}q^{\prime}
or
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x+1}q
.
Now for each priority
y
, close the relations
\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:y}
by transitivity, which does not augment the language.
Moreover, for priorities
y\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}y^{\prime}
(recall that
1\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}3\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}\dots\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}d+1\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}d\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}\dots\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}2\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\preccurlyeq}}0
) add transition
q\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:y}q^{\prime}
whenever
\mathcal{A}
contains
q\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:y^{\prime}}q^{\prime}
; this also does not augment the language.
Then it holds that the relations
\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:1},\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:3},\dots,\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:d+1}
are
total preorders

refining
one another, and that for each even
x
,
\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x}
is the strict variant of
\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x+1}
.
Stated differently, the obtained automaton
\mathcal{A}
is an
\varepsilon
-completion
of
\mathcal{A}_{0}
, which implies that
W
is
positional
thanks to Theorem
23
.

Note that on the way, we obtain the following result as an interesting consequence.

Corollary 111
.

Any
non-deterministic

parity automaton

recognising
a
positional
language is
\varepsilon
-completable
.

We now prove Theorem
110
.
The proof is inspired by that of
[
24
, Theorem 4.8]
, but it is more involved, because we now deal with
parity automata
rather than graphs (or safety automata).
This difficulty is overcome thanks to Theorem
27
.

Proof of Theorem
110
.

Fix a pair of states
q,q^{\prime}\in Q
and an even
priority

x
.
Consider the
game

\mathcal{G}
defined as follows (see also Figure
18
below).

•

The alphabet is
C=(\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\})\times\{0,1,\dots,d+1\}\times\{\text{enter}_{q},\text{small},\text{neutral}\}
.
Therefore, each edge has a letter in
\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}
, a priority in
\{0,1,\dots,d+1\}
, and a type in
\{\text{enter}_{q},\text{small},\text{neutral}\}
.
For a word
w\in C^{\omega}
, we write
w_{\Sigma},w_{\mathsf{prio}}
and
w_{\mathsf{type}}
for the respective projections.
For conciseness, we generally omit the type and write edges in the game as
\xrightarrow{a:y}
, just like in the automaton.

•

The set of vertices consists in two copies of
\mathcal{A}
indexed by
q
and
q^{\prime}
, together with an additional vertex
q_{?}
.
Formally,
V=Q\times\{q,q^{\prime}\}\cup\{q_{?}\}
.
All vertices belong to
Adam
except for
q_{?}
which belongs to
Eve
.

•

The edges in the copy indexed by
q
(resp.
q^{\prime}
) follow exactly the transitions in
\mathcal{A}
, except those leading to
q^{\prime}
(resp.
q
), which are instead redirected to
q_{?}
(but keep the same letter and priority).

•

The vertex
q_{?}
has exactly two outgoing edges:
q_{?}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x+1}(q,q)
and
q_{?}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x}(q^{\prime},q^{\prime})
.

•

The edge
q_{?}\xrightarrow{\varepsilon:x+1}(q,q)
has type
\text{enter}_{q}
, and edges with priority
\leq x
inside the copy indexed by
q
have type
small
. All other edges are neutral.

•

The objective is

W_{\mathcal{G}}=W_{\Sigma}\cup{\mathsf{oddParity}}\cup{\mathsf{goodType}},

where
W_{\Sigma}
is the set of words
w
such that
w_{\Sigma}\in W
,
{\mathsf{oddParity}}
is the set of words whose minimal priority appearing infinitely often is odd, and
{\mathsf{goodType}}
is the set of words with infinitely many occurrences of type
\text{enter}_{q}
and finitely many occurrences of type
small
.

Figure 18:
The
game

\mathcal{G}
. Edges which are crossed out are those that are redirected (while keeping the same label). Note that
(q^{\prime},q)
and
(q,q^{\prime})
are not reachable; these vertices could be removed from the game.

Clearly
W_{\Sigma}
is
positional
and so is
{\mathsf{oddParity}}
; likewise,
{\mathsf{goodType}}
rewrites as a
parity condition
(by mapping
small
to 1,
\text{enter}_{q}
to 2 and
neutral
to 3), and thus it is also
positional
.
Moreover,
{\mathsf{oddParity}}
and
{\mathsf{goodType}}
are
prefix-independent
. It follows from Theorem
27
that
W^{\prime}
is positional.

priorities

\pi_{\mathcal{G}}
eventually coincide with those in
\pi_{\mathcal{A}}
, and since this is a
rejecting run
in
\mathcal{A}
,
\pi_{\mathcal{G}}
satisfies
{\mathsf{oddParity}}
.

•

small
, then the minimal

appearing infinitely often in

, therefore adding (even infinitely many) priorities

satisfies

.

defines a path in
\mathcal{G}
which is consistent with
\sigma
.
Therefore the label of
\pi_{\mathcal{G}}
satisfies
W_{\mathcal{G}}
.
Note that
priorities
in
\pi_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime}}
and
\pi_{\mathcal{G}}
are the same, and
\pi_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime}}
is
accepting
, therefore
\pi_{\mathcal{G}}
does not satisfy
{\mathsf{oddParity}}
.

Now note that
\pi_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime}}
has infinitely many occurrences of priority
x+1
and yet it is
accepting
, therefore it has infinitely many occurrences of priorities
\leq x
.
Thus
\pi_{\mathcal{G}}
has infinitely many occurrences of
small
, so it does not satisfy
{\mathsf{goodType}}
.
We conclude that
\pi_{\mathcal{G}}
satisfies
W_{\Sigma}
, and therefore the label
w_{0}a_{0}w_{1}a_{1}\dots
of
\pi_{\mathcal{A}^{\prime}}
belongs to
W
.

This concludes the proof.
∎

Remark 115
.

It is interesting to remark that our proof relies on the fact that for any
\omega
-regular

positional

objective

W
, the
objective

W\cup{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{parity}}
is
positional
.
We do not know a direct proof of this fact (without using Theorem
27
which relies on the machinery employed to prove Theorem
23
).
Such a direct proof would give, together with Theorem
110
, an easier path to the main characterisation and the polynomial time decidability (though it would fall short of establishing the 1-to-2-player lift and the finite-to-infinite lift).

7
Bipositionality of all objectives

In this section we provide a characterisation of all
bipositional
objectives, without
\omega
-regularity
or
prefix-independence
assumptions.
This characterisation extends the result of Colcombet and Niwiński
[
26
]
, who showed that the only
prefix-independent

bipositional
objective (over all game graphs) is the
parity objective
.
Recently, Bouyer, Randour and Vandenhove
[
12
]
generalised that result in an orthogonal direction: they proved that the only objectives for which both players can
play optimally using
finite chromatic memory are
\omega
-regular objectives
.

7.1
Characterisation of bipositionality and consequences

We say that an objective
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
is
bi-progress consistent
if both
W
and its complement are
progress consistent
, that is, if it satisfies that for all
residual class

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[u]}
and finite word
w\in\Sigma^{*}
:

•

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[u]}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[uw]}\implies uw^{\omega}\in W
, and

•

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[uw]}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[u]}\implies uw^{\omega}\notin W
.

Theorem 116

(Characterisation of bipositionality)
.

An objective
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
is
bipositional
(over all games) if and only if:

1.

W
has a finite number of
residuals
, totally ordered by inclusion, and

2.

W
is
bi-progress consistent
, and

3.

W
can be
recognised
by a
parity automaton on top of
the
automaton of residuals
.

This characterisation only holds for infinite games, as there are non
\omega
-regular

objectives
that are
bipositional
over finite games, as, for example, energy objectives
[
10
]
and their generalisation
[
36
]
. However, we deduce from Theorem
26
that in the case of
\omega
-regular
objectives these conditions do also characterise
bipositionality
over finite games.

Corollary 117

(Bipositionality over finite games for
\omega
-regular objectives)
.

An
\omega
-regular
objective
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
is
bipositional
over finite games if and only if it satisfies the three conditions from Theorem
116
.

Consequences: Lifts and decidability

For
\omega
-regular objectives
, we can directly lift the corollaries of Theorem
23
obtained for
positionality
to
bipositionality
. For non-
\omega
-regular ones, the finite-to-infinite lift does not hold, as commented above. On the other hand, a combination with a recent result from Bouyer, Randour and Vandenhove
[
12
, Theorem 3.8]
implies that the 1-to-2-player lift holds for any objective.

We say that an objective
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
is
bipositional over (finite) Eve and Adam-games
if both
W
and its complement
\Sigma^{\omega}\setminus W
are
positional
over (finite)
Eve-games
.

Corollary 118

(1-to-2 player lift of bipositionality)
.

An objective
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
is
bipositional
(over all games) if and only if it is
bipositional over Eve and Adam-games
.

We note that a 1-to-2 player lift was obtained for objectives that are
bipositional
over finite game graphs by Gimbert and Zielonka
[
31
,
53
]
(even in the more general setting of qualitative objectives).
However, their proof consisted in an induction over the size of the game graph, so it does not generalise to infinite games.
Indeed, as remarked above,
bipositionality
over finite and infinite graphs behaves in a completely different manner.
In this respect, Corollary
118
and the result of Gimbert and Zielonka are incomparable.

Corollary 119

(Finite-to-infinite lift of bipositionality for
\omega
-regular objectives)
.

An
\omega
-regular
objective
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
is
bipositional
(over all games) if and only if it is
bipositional over finite Eve and Adam-games
.

We obtain decidability for
bipositionality
in polynomial time from its counterpart in the case of
positionality
(Theorem
25
). We observe that Theorem
116
provides an alternative way to check
bipositionality
.

Corollary 120

(Decidability of bipositionality)
.

Given a
deterministic

parity automaton

\mathcal{A}
, we can decide in polynomial time whether
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}
is
bipositional
.

An example

Example 121

(Parity over occurrences)
.

We let
\Sigma=[0,d]
and let
\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}W_{\mathsf{OccParity}}}
be the language of words such that the minimal
priority
appearing on them is even:

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{\mathsf{OccParity}}}=\{w\in[0,d]^{\omega}\mid\min(w)\text{ is even}\}.

An automaton
recognising

W
is depicted in Figure
19
. It has one state per
residual
, which are totally ordered, and it is immediate to check that it is
bi-progress consistent
. Therefore,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{\mathsf{OccParity}}}
is a
bipositional
objective.

Figure 19:
Automaton
recognising

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{\mathsf{OccParity}}}
, for
d=4
. The initial state is
q_{4}
. This automaton is in fact what is sometimes called a weak automaton: runs that finally end in an even state are
accepting
, and those ending in an odd state are
rejecting
.

Some more complex examples can be generated by, for example, adding some output priorities to the automaton above without breaking the
bi-progress consistency
condition. However, the combination of being recognisable by the
automaton of residuals
with
bi-progress consistency
greatly restricts the possibilities of generating examples of
bipositional
languages. We wonder whether a more precise characterisation of languages satisfying these three properties can be obtained.

7.2
Proof of the characterisation

Necessity of the conditions

The necessity of the total order over the residuals of
W
is given by Lemma
33
, and the necessity of
bi-progress consistency
is given by Lemma
38
.
The following lemma provides the necessity of the last condition of Theorem
116
.
It can be obtained by instantiating the first item of
[
12
, Theorem 3.6]
for the case of
bipositional
objectives.

Lemma 122

(
[
12
, Theorem 3.6]
)
.

If
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
is
bipositional over Eve and Adam-games
, then
W
is
\omega
-regular
and can be
recognised
by a
parity automaton
on top of the
automaton of residuals
.

Sufficiency of the conditions

The sufficiency of conditions of Theorem
116
can be shown by providing
well-ordered

monotone

universal
graphs for
W
and its complement.
An even simpler option – now that we have already done such construction for
positional
objectives – is to provide
fully progress consistent

signature automata
recognising these languages, and then use the characterisation of
positionality
given by Item
(6)
from Theorem
23
.

We show that the
parity automaton on top
of the
automaton of residuals
is a
fully progress consistent

signature automata
. Since by hypothesis
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is totally ordered, the order
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{0}}
given by inclusion of
residuals
satisfies the first requirement of the definition of
signature automaton
. As the
residual classes
of this automaton are trivial, we can define all relations
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
to be trivial too, so this automaton satisfies all the requirements to be a
signature automaton
.
Moreover, as
W
is
progress consistent
and the
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-classes of the automaton are trivial, it is also
fully progress consistent
.
The argument is symmetric for
\Sigma^{\omega}\setminus W
.

8
Positionality of closed and open objectives

8.1
Closed objectives

We recall that an objective
W
is
closed
if

W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safety}(L)}=\{w\mid w\text{ does not contain any prefix in }L\},

for some language of finite words
L
.

Positional

closed objectives
were first characterised by Colcombet, Fijalkow and Horn
[
25
]
, as those that have a totally ordered set of residuals.
However, as they already remarked, this characterisation only holds for finite branching
game graphs
.

We now give a characterisation of
positionality
over all game graphs for
closed objectives
.
Namely, a
closed objective

W
is
positional
if and only if
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is well-ordered by inclusion (Theorem
126
) (in fact, the well-foundedness of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is a necessary condition for finite memory determinacy of any objective.)
This (and its generalisation to memory) was already observed in
[
22
]
.

8.1.1
Well-foundedness of residuals

Next example, taken from
[
25
]
, shows that total order over residuals does not suffice to ensure
positionality
of arbitrary
closed objectives
.

Example 123

(Outbidding game
[
25
]
: Total order does not suffice)
.

Let
\Sigma=\{a,b,c\}
and
L
be the language of finite words:

L=\{w\in\Sigma^{*}\mid\text{ for some }u\in\Sigma^{*}\text{ with }{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}|u|_{a}}\leq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}|u|_{b}},uc\text{ is a prefix of }w\},

where
\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}|u|_{x}}
is the number of occurrences of
a
in
u
.
We consider the
closed objective

W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safety}(L)}
.
The
residuals
of
W
are totally ordered by inclusion:

\emptyset={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}c}^{-1}W<\dots<{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(a^{n})}^{-1}W<\cdots<{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}a}^{-1}W<{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\varepsilon}^{-1}W<{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}b}^{-1}W<\cdots.

However,
W
is not
positional
, as witnessed by the game in Figure
20
.

Figure 20:
Outbidding game. First, a sequence
a^{n}
is produced, for some
n\in\mathbb{N}
. In order to win,
Eve
needs to answer with
b^{m}
, with
m>n
. Therefore, she can win from any vertex in the game, but no
positional strategy
guarantees the victory from all states.

Lemma 124

(Necessity of the well-order of residuals)
.

Let
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
be an
objective
that is
positional
over
\varepsilon
-free

Eve-games
. Then,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is well-ordered by inclusion.

We have already seen (Lemma
33
), that if
W
is
positional
, then
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is totally ordered. We need to prove that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is well-founded.

Lemma 125

(Well-foundedness of residuals necessary for finite memory)
.

Let
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
be an
objective
such that
Eve
can
play optimally using positional strategies
(or using finite memory strategies) over
\varepsilon
-free

Eve-games
. Then,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is well-founded (for the order given by inclusion of
residuals
).

Proof.

Suppose by contradiction that there is an infinite strictly decreasing sequence of
residuals
:

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{1}}^{-1}W\supsetneq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{2}}^{-1}W\supsetneq\cdots,\;u_{i}\in\Sigma^{*}.

(We suppose without loss of generality that
\varepsilon\neq u_{i}
for all
i
.)
Let
w_{i}\in\Sigma^{\omega}
such that
w_{i}\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{i}}^{-1}W\setminus{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{i+1}}^{-1}W
.
We consider the game – similar to the outbidding game from Figure
20
– in which a word
u_{i}
labels a path from a vertex
v_{i}
to
v_{\mathsf{choice}}
, for each
i
. From this latter vertex,
Eve
can choose a between paths labelled by
\{w_{i}\mid i\in\mathbb{N}\}
.

Eve
can win be answering
w_{i}
to
u_{i}
. However, any
positional
(or finite memory) strategy will only consider a finite number of responses
w_{j_{1}},\dots,w_{j_{n}}
. Therefore, such a strategy is
losing
from
v_{K}
for
K>\max\{j_{t}\mid 1\leq t\leq n\}
. ∎

8.1.2
Characterisation for closed objectives

Theorem 126

(Positional closed objectives)
.

Let
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
be a
closed objective
. Then,
W
is
positional
(over all
game graphs
) if and only if
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is well-ordered by inclusion.

Proof.

We have already shown that this condition is necessary. To prove sufficiency, we give, for each cardinal
\kappa
, a
(\kappa,W)
-universal

well-ordered

monotone
graph. We conclude by Proposition
4
.

Let
U
be the
\Sigma
-graph
that has as vertices
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}\setminus\{\emptyset\}
, ordered by inclusion. By hypothesis, this is a well-order. For each
a\in\Sigma
, we let

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u}^{-1}W\xrightarrow{a}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u^{\prime}}^{-1}W\;\;\text{ iff }\;\;{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u^{\prime}}^{-1}W\leq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(ua)}^{-1}W.

We note that if
ua
is already losing (
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(ua)}^{-1}W=\emptyset
), then transition
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u}^{-1}W\xrightarrow{a}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u^{\prime}}^{-1}W
does not appear in
U
.
By Lemma
19
, graph
U
is
monotone
.
The hypothesis of
closeness
of
W
is fundamentally used in next claim.

Claim 127
.

A vertex
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u}^{-1}W
of
U

satisfies

W
if and only if
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u}^{-1}W\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\varepsilon}^{-1}W=W
.

{claimproof}

Let
L\subseteq\Sigma^{*}
such that
W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safety}(L)}
. Let

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{1}}^{-1}W\xrightarrow{a_{1}}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{2}}^{-1}W\xrightarrow{a_{2}}\dots

be a path in
U
from
u_{1}=u
. By induction we obtain
\emptyset\neq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{i}}^{-1}W\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(u_{1}a_{1}\dots a_{i-1})}^{-1}W
.
Therefore, for all
i
,
ua_{1}\dots a_{i}\notin L
, so, by definition of
W
, the infinite word
ua_{1}a_{2}\dots
belongs to
W
.

We show that
U
is
(\kappa,W)
-universal for trees
, for every cardinal
\kappa
, and conclude by Lemma
5
.
Let
T
be a
\Sigma
-tree
which
satisfies

W
. For each node
t\in T
, let
\phi(t)={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{t}}^{-1}W
be the minimal
residual
such that
t

satisfies

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{t}}^{-1}W
. In particular, for the
root

t_{0}
,
\phi(t_{0})

satisfies

W
by the previous claim.
We claim that
\phi
is a
morphism
. Indeed, if
t\xrightarrow{a}t^{\prime}
in
T
and
t

satisfies

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u}^{-1}W
, then
t^{\prime}

satisfies

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(ua)}^{-1}W
. Therefore,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{t}^{\prime}}^{-1}W\leq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(u_{t}a)}^{-1}W
, so
\phi(t)={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{t}}^{-1}W\xrightarrow{a}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{t^{\prime}}}^{-1}W=\phi(t^{\prime})
is an edge in
U
.
∎

8.2
Open objectives

We recall that an objective
W
is
open
if

W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Reach}(L)}=\{w\mid w\text{ contains some prefix in }L\},

for some
L\subseteq\Sigma^{*}
.

8.2.1
Reset-stability

In Section
4.2
, we showed that
positional

\omega
-regular

open
objectives are exactly those with residuals totally ordered and that are
progress consistent
. However, for
non-
\omega
-regular
objectives, these conditions do not suffice, even if residuals are well-ordered.

Example 128

(Progress consistency does not suffice)
.

Let
\Sigma=\mathbb{N}
and let
W
be the set of non strictly increasing sequences:

W=\{a_{1}a_{2}\dots\in\mathbb{N}^{\omega}\mid a_{i+1}\leq a_{i}\text{ for some }i\ \}.

This objective is
open
, as
W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Reach}(\text{two consecutive non-increasing numbers})}
. Its residuals are:

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\varepsilon}^{-1}W<{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}0}^{-1}W<{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}1}^{-1}W<{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}2}^{-1}W<\cdots<{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(00)}^{-1}W=\Sigma^{\omega}.

Therefore,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is well-ordered. Moreover,
W
is
progress consistent
: any repetition of factors induces a non-strict inequality
<
between consecutive letters.

However, we claim that
W
is not
positional
. Consider the game in Figure
21
.

Eve
can win this game: no matter what is the vertex
v_{i}
chosen by
Adam
, she can first move one position to the right, producing
i
, and then go down producing letter
1
. This ensures two consecutive non-increasing numbers.
However, she cannot
win positionally
. Indeed, if such a strategy tells her to go always to the left, the sequence produced will be strictly increasing. If she choses to go down in vertex
v_{i}
, Adam can win by initialising the play in that vertex.

Figure 21:
Game in which Eve wins if she produces a non-strictly increasing sequence of numbers. She can win from every vertex, but not positionally.

Definition 129

(Reset-stability)
.

We say that an
objective

W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
is
reset-stable
if, for each sequence of finite words
u_{1},u_{2},u_{3},\dots\in\Sigma^{+}
and of residuals
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}s_{0}}^{-1}W,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}s_{1}}^{-1}W,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}s_{2}}^{-1}W,\dots\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
:

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}s_{i}}^{-1}W\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(s_{i-1}u_{i})}^{-1}W\;\text{ for all }i\geq 1\;\;\implies\;\;u_{1}u_{2}u_{3}\dots\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}s_{0}}^{-1}W.

An intuitive idea of
reset-stability
is the following. Consider the (potentially infinite)
automaton of residuals
of
W
, which inherits the order over residuals. Add to it all
\varepsilon
-transitions going backwards:
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}s}^{-1}W\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}s^{\prime}}^{-1}W
for
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}s^{\prime}}^{-1}W<{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}s}^{-1}W
. When a run takes an
\varepsilon
-transition, we say that it
makes a reset
.
What
reset-stability
tells us is that any run making infinitely many resets must be accepting. The words
u_{1},u_{2},\dots
in the definition above correspond to fragments where no
reset
takes place, and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}s_{i}}^{-1}W
is the
residual
where we land after the i
th

reset
.
(See also the notion of
0
-jumps
in the proof of Lemma
99
).

Remark 130
.

If
W
is
reset-stable
, it is
progress consistent
. The converse holds if
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is finite and totally ordered.

We note that all
closed objectives
are
reset-stable
.

Lemma 131

(Necessity of reset-stability)
.

Let
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
be a
positional

objective
over
\varepsilon
-free

Eve-games
. Then,
W
is
reset-stable
.

Proof.

Suppose by contradiction that
W
is not
reset-stable
. That is, there are
u_{1},u_{2},\dots\Sigma^{+}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}s_{0}}^{-1}W,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}s_{1}}^{-1}W\dots
such that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}s_{i}}^{-1}W<{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(s_{i-1}u_{i})}^{-1}W
, but
u_{1}u_{2}\dots\notin{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}s_{0}}^{-1}W
.

Let
w_{i}\in\Sigma^{\omega}
such that
w_{i}\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(s_{i-1}u_{i})}^{-1}W\setminus{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}s_{i}}^{-1}W
.
We consider the game pictured in Figure
22
(to ensure it to be
\varepsilon
-free
, we just remove vertex
v_{i}
if
s_{i}=\varepsilon
).

Figure 22:
Game in which Eve wins if she produces a non-strictly increasing sequence of numbers. She can win from every
v_{i}
, but not positionally.

Eve
can win
\mathcal{G}
from any vertex
v_{i}
(and from
v_{i}^{\prime}
if
s_{i}=\varepsilon
), as she can produce the word
s_{i}u_{i+1}w_{i+1}
, which belongs to
W
, as we have taken
w_{i+1}\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(s_{i}u_{i+1})}^{-1}W
.
However, we show that no
positional strategy
ensures to win from all these vertices.
We distinguish two cases. If this
strategy
takes the path
v_{i}^{\prime}\mathrel{\hbox to21.54pt{\vbox to10.25pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 10.77162pt\lower-5.67638pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

8.2.2
Characterisation for open objectives

Theorem 132

(Positional open objectives)
.

Let
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
be an
open objective
. Then,
W
is
positional
(over all
game graphs
) if and only if:

•

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is well-ordered by inclusion, and

•

W
is
reset-stable
.

Proof.

The necessity of the conditions has already been established in Lemmas
125
and
131
. To prove the sufficiency, we give, for each cardinal
\kappa
, a
well-ordered

monotone
graph that is
(\kappa,W)
-universal for trees
, and conclude by Proposition
4
and Lemma
5
.

We let
U
be the
\Sigma
-graph
having as set of vertices
({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}\setminus\{\emptyset\})\times\kappa
, ordered lexicographically. This graph is
well-ordered
, as by hypothesis so is
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
. The edges are given by:

({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u}^{-1}W,\lambda)\,\xrightarrow{a}\,({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u^{\prime}}^{-1}W,\lambda^{\prime})\quad\text{ if }\quad\left\{\begin{array}[]{lc}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u^{\prime}}^{-1}W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(ua)}^{-1}W\text{ and }\lambda^{\prime}<\lambda,&\text{ or }\\[5.69054pt]
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u^{\prime}}^{-1}W\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(ua)}^{-1}W,&\text{ or }\\[5.69054pt]
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u}^{-1}W=\Sigma^{\omega}.&\end{array}\right.

By Lemma
19
, this graph is
monotone
. We show its
(\kappa,W)
-universality for trees
. The key ingredient for this is next claim, which strongly relies in the
reset-stability
hypothesis.
We let
L
be the language of finite words such that
W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Reach}(L)}
.

Claim 133
.

For each ordinal
\lambda<\kappa
and each
residual

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u}^{-1}W
, vertex
({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u}^{-1}W,\lambda)

satisfies

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u}^{-1}W
in
U
.

{claimproof}

Let
\rho=({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{0}}^{-1}W,\lambda_{0})\xrightarrow{a_{1}}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{1}}^{-1}W,\lambda_{1})\xrightarrow{a_{1}}\cdots
be an infinite path from
({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u}^{-1}W,\lambda)
in
U
, and consider its projection over the (infinite)
automaton of residuals

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{R}}_{W}
. Whenever
\rho
takes a transition
({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{i}}^{-1}W,\lambda_{i})\,\xrightarrow{a}_{i}\,({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u{i+1}}^{-1}W,\lambda_{i+1})
with
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{i+1}}^{-1}W={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(u_{i}a_{i})}^{-1}W
, this transition exists in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{R}}_{W}
. If
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{i+1}}^{-1}W\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}<}}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(u_{i}a_{i})}^{-1}W
, we say that this transition
makes a reset
.
By induction, we obtain that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{i}}^{-1}W\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(ua_{1}\dots a_{i})}^{-1}W
. We distinguish two cases:
(1) If
\rho

makes infinitely many resets
, then we conclude by
reset-stability
. (2) If
\rho

makes finitely many resets
, then eventually
\lambda_{i+1}<\lambda_{i}
for all
i
, unless
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{i}}^{-1}W=\Sigma^{\omega}
. We conclude that eventually
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{i}}^{-1}W=\Sigma^{\omega}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(ua_{1}\dots a_{i})}^{-1}W
. Therefore,
ua_{1}\dots a_{i}\in L
, so
ua_{1}a_{2}\dots\in W
.

Let
T
be a
\Sigma
-tree
whose
root

satisfies

W
.
We give a
morphism

\phi\colon T\to U
, which we decompose in
\phi_{1}\colon T\to{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}\setminus\{\emptyset\}
and
\phi_{2}\colon T\to\kappa
.
For each
t\in T
, let
u_{t}
be the word labelling the path from the
root

t_{0}
to
t
. We let
\phi_{1}(t)={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{t}}^{-1}W
for each
t
.
We define
\phi_{2}
by transfinite induction.
By hypothesis, each branch eventually contains vertices
t
such that
u_{t}\in L
(that is,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{t}^{-1}=}\Sigma^{\omega}
). For all these vertices, we let
\phi_{2}(t)=0
.
The tree obtained by removing these vertices, named
T_{1}
, does not have any infinite branch.
For an ordinal
\lambda<\kappa
, let
T_{\lambda}
be the set of nodes for which we have not defined
\phi_{2}
at step
\lambda
of the induction.
For each leaf
t
of
T_{\lambda}
, we let
\phi_{2}(t)=\lambda
.

This mapping has the two following properties:

•

if
t\xrightarrow{a}t^{\prime}
in
T
, then
\phi_{1}(t^{\prime})={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}(u_{t}a)}^{-1}W
, and

•

if
t\xrightarrow{a}t^{\prime}
in
T
, either
\phi_{2}(t^{\prime})<\phi_{2}(t)
, or
u_{t^{\prime}}\in L
.

This ensures that
\phi=(\phi_{1},\phi_{2})
is a
morphism
, concluding the proof.
∎

Example 134

(Positional open objective)
.

Let
\Sigma=\mathbb{N}
and let
W
be the set of sequences that start by
123\dots n
, and eventually decrease. Formally:

W=\{a_{1}a_{2}\dots\in\mathbb{N}^{\omega}\mid\text{there is }j\text{ such that }a_{i}=i\text{ for }i<j\text{ and }a_{j}<j\}.

This objective is
recognised
by the infinite reachability automaton depicted in Figure
23
.
Its residuals are well-ordered and it is
reset-stable
, as after any reset we necessarily produce an word in
W
. Therefore,
W
is
positional
.

We remark that this objective is not
bipositional
, as
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(\Sigma^{\omega}\setminus W)}
is not well-founded. This contrast with the case of
\omega
-regular open
objectives, for which all
positional

open objectives
are
bipositional
(Corollary
42
).

Figure 23:
Game in which Eve wins if she produces a non-strictly increasing sequence of numbers. She can win, but not positionally.

8.3
1-to-2-player lift and addition of neutral letters

Corollary 135

(1-to-2-player lift for open and closed objectives)
.

Let
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
be an
open
or
closed

objective
. If
W
is
positional
over
\varepsilon
-free

Eve-games
, then
W
is
positional
over all
game graphs
.

We also obtain from our proofs that the Neutral letter conjecture (Conjecture
31
) holds for
open
and
closed
objectives.

Corollary 136

(Closure under addition of neutral letters)
.

Let
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
be an
open
or
closed

objective
. If
W
is
positional
, then
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W^{\varepsilon}}
is
positional
.

Proof.

In the proof of Theorems
126
and
132
, we obtained the positionality of objectives by providing
well-ordered

monotone

(\kappa,W)
-universal
graphs. Proposition
30
allows us to conclude.
∎

We have therefore obtained the 1-to-2-player lift for
\omega
-regular objectives, as well as
open
and
closed
ones.
However, the 1-to-2-player lift does not hold for arbitrary objectives.
A counter-example is discussed in the PhD of Pierre Vandenhove
[
51
, p.236]
.
11
11

11

In his PhD
[
51
]
, Vandenhove discusses the 1-to-2-player lift for finite
game graphs
. The counter-example he gives also applies to infinite
game graphs
.
The objective considered there (first appearing in
[
34
]
), is:

\mathbf{MP}^{\mathbb{Q}}=\{w\in\{0,1\}^{\omega}\mid\liminf_{n}\large(\sum_{i=0}^{n}w_{i}\large)\large/n\;\;\text{ is rational}\}.

We provide here a different example.

Proposition 137

(No general 1-to-2-player lift)
.

There is an objective
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
that is
positional
over
Eve-games
, but is not
positional
over all
game graphs
.

Proof.

Let
\Sigma
be any infinite alphabet, and let
W
be the following objective:

\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}W_{\mathsf{fin}}}=\{w\in\Sigma^{\omega}\mid\text{ the set of letters occurring infinitely often in }w\text{ is finite}\}.

To show that it is not
positional
, we consider the game in Figure
24
, in which
Eve
controls a single vertex, from which she can send the token to any vertex
v_{i}
controlled by
Adam
.

Figure 24:
Game in which Eve wins if only finitely many letters are produced infinitely often. She can win by sending the token further and further away, but she cannot
win positionally
.

We claim that
Eve
can win this game from every vertex by using the following
strategy
: she keeps track of the maximal index
i_{\max}
such that the play has passed trough vertex
v_{i_{\max}}
. Whenever Adam sends back the token to
v_{\mathrm{Eve}}
, she will go to vertex
v_{i_{\max}}
. This
strategy
ensures that only letter
1
will be produced infinitely often.

However,
Eve
cannot win using a
positional
(or even finite memory) strategy. Such a strategy will only consider finitely many edges
v_{\mathrm{Eve}}\xrightarrow{1}v_{i}
. Let
v_{k}
be the maximal such vertex.
Adam
can win against such strategy by producing longer and longer paths, and then sending back the token to the vertex controlled by
Eve
:
v_{i}\mathrel{\hbox to39.08pt{\vbox to14.41pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 19.54175pt\lower-7.75276pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}
