. In this way, all numbers greater that
k
will be produced infinitely often.

We show that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{\mathsf{fin}}}
is positional over
Eve-games
.

Claim 138
.

For every
Eve-game

\mathcal{G}
with
winning condition

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{\mathsf{fin}}}
and every fixed vertex
v_{0}
, if
Eve
wins from
v_{0}
, she can
win from
v_{0}
using a
positional strategy
.

{claimproof}

Assume that
Eve

wins from
v_{0}
.
A
strategy
from
v_{0}
is just an infinite path from
v
. Consider such a path. If this path does not visit a same vertex twice, it is already a positional strategy. On the contrary, let
v_{k}
be the first vertex that repeats. Consider the first two occurrences of
v_{\mathsf{rep}}
:

v_{0}\xrightarrow{a_{0}}v_{1}\xrightarrow{a_{1}}\cdots v_{k}\xrightarrow{a_{k}}\cdots v_{k+j}\xrightarrow{a_{k+j}}v_{k}.

Then, the
positional strategy
indicating to take the edge
v_{i}\xrightarrow{a_{i}}v_{i+1}
for
i\leq k+j
is
winning
.

We use this claim to prove that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{\mathsf{fin}}}
is (
uniformly
)
positional
over
Eve-games
.
Let
\mathcal{G}
be an
Eve-game
with
winning condition

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{\mathsf{fin}}}
. By
prefix-independence
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{\mathsf{fin}}}
, we can suppose without loss of generality that
Eve

wins from
every vertex in
\mathcal{G}
. Let
v_{1},v_{2},\dots
a (potentially transfinite) enumeration of vertices in
\mathcal{G}
. We will define a positional strategy
\mathsf{strat}\colon V\to E
by transfinite induction. At step
\lambda
, let
\mathcal{G}_{\lambda}
be the game obtained by removing vertices for which
\mathsf{strat}
has already been defined. Let
i
be the minimal index such that
v_{i}
appears in
\mathcal{G}_{\lambda}
. By the previous claim,
Eve
has a positional strategy in
\mathcal{G}_{\lambda}
that wins from
v_{i}
. Let
V_{\lambda}
be the vertices reachable from
v
by using this strategy, and for
v\in V_{\lambda}
let
\mathsf{strat}(v)
be the edge indicated by such strategy. We let
V_{\lambda}^{\prime}
be the vertices in
\mathcal{G}_{\lambda}\setminus V_{\lambda}
from which
Eve
can reach
V_{\lambda}
, and fix a positional strategy doing so. We let
\mathsf{strat}(v^{\prime})
being given by this strategy for these vertices.
It is immediate that
\mathsf{strat}
is a
positional strategy
in
\mathcal{G}
that
wins from
all vertices.
∎

9
Conclusions

The results presented in Section
3
effectively address most open questions regarding
positionality
in the context of
\omega
-regular languages
.
Yet, it would be reasonable to seek a “better” characterisation.
One drawback of our approach is its conceptual complexity and its exclusive focus on automata; the characterisation is based on syntactic and combinatorial properties of
parity automata
, rather than on intrinsic language-theoretical properties of the languages they
recognise
.
In this respect, the insights gained about
positionality
are somewhat limited.
Therefore, we believe that there is still room for improvement and for a deeper understanding of the class of
positional

\omega
-regular
objectives.

To conclude, we discuss further research directions extending our results.

9.1
Positionality of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{BC}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma_{2}^{0}})}
languages

A potential research direction consists in investigating
positionality
for broader classes of objectives.
We initiated this path in Section
8
by studying
positionality
of
closed
and
open
objectives.
Going further in that direction, the goal is to develop characterisations for more complex objectives defined by topological properties, mainly, higher classes in the Borel hierarchy.
A natural first step could be to look at objectives in
\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}\Sigma_{2}^{0}}
and
\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}\Pi_{2}^{0}}
, which are, respectively, unions of closed objectives and intersections of open objectives. These classes admit automata-oriented definitions:
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma_{2}^{0}}
are the objectives
recognised
by
deterministic
infinite
Büchi automata
, and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Pi_{2}^{0}}
those
recognised
by infinite
coBüchi automata

[
47
]
.
Recently, Ohlmann and Skrzypczak proposed a characterisation of
positionality
for
prefix-independent
objectives in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma_{2}^{0}}
; however the cases of non-
prefix-independent

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma_{2}^{0}}

objectives
or
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Pi_{2}^{0}}

objectives
are open.

The class of objectives
recognised
by infinite
deterministic
parity automata coincides with

\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}\mathcal{BC}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma_{2}^{0}})}
: the class of boolean combinations of objectives in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma_{2}^{0}}

[
47
]
(this is a strict subclass of
\Delta_{3}^{0}=\Sigma_{3}^{0}\cap\Pi_{3}^{0}
). We hope to be able to give a characterisation for this class – as some of the constructions introduced in this work seems to generalise to automata with infinite states.
We believe that some properties of
positional

\omega
-regular objectives
could be lifted to
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{BC}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma_{2}^{0}})}
(or even to
\Delta_{3}
). In particular, we conjecture that the 1-to-2 player lift (false in general, see Proposition
137
), holds for
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{BC}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma_{2}^{0}})}
-objectives.

Conjecture 139

(1-to-2 player lift in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{BC}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma_{2}^{0}})}
)
.

Let
W
be an objective in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{BC}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma_{2}^{0}})}
that is
positional over

Eve-games
. Then, it is
positional
over all games.

Decidability problems lose their relevance when dealing with classes of objectives defined by topological properties. Therefore, the question of what is a satisfactory characterisation becomes even harder to answer in this context – especially when taking into account that we already have Ohlmann’s characterisation based on
universal graphs

[
44
]
.
A important steps forward would involve proving Conjecture
139
, as well as
Kopczyński’s conjecture
(Conjecture
1
) or Ohlmann’s
neutral letter conjecture
(Conjecture
31
) for the class
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{BC}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma_{2}^{0}})}
.

9.2
Memory requirements of
\omega
-regular languages

An orthogonal research direction would be to maintain the focus on
\omega
-regular languages
, but attempt to characterise their memory requirements rather than just their
positionality
.
A notable effort has already been made in this direction
[
27
,
34
,
25
,
11
,
17
,
20
]
,
however, only characterisations for fairly simple classes of languages are known (Muller
[
27
]
and
closed languages

[
25
]
).
To this day, deciding whether
Eve
can
play optimally
in (finite or infinite) games using a given
\omega
-regular objective
(even an
open
one) with
\leq k
states of memory is not know to be decidable.
Also, the versions of the 1-to-2-players and finite-to-infinite lifts in the case of memory remain open (see
[
51
, Conjecture 9.1.1]
).

One difficulty is the multiplicity of models of memory: general, chromatic,
\varepsilon
-memory… (we refer to
[
18
, Chapter IV]
for details).
Recently, Bouyer, Fijalkow, Randour and Vandenhove showed that computing the chromatic memory requirements of
\omega
-regular

open
and
closed
objectives is
\mathsf{NP}\mathchar 45\relax\mathrm{complete}

[
11
]
.
This result, together with the
\mathsf{NP}
-completeness of the computation of the chromatic memory requirements of Muller objectives
[
17
]
, indicates that chromatic memory might be an ill-suited model for these purposes.
We believe that the most promising model to focus on in order to advance on this problem is
\varepsilon
-memory, as discussed in
[
22
]
.
A first step required for moving forward involves characterising memory requirements for
open objectives
. Nevertheless, progress in understanding the general memory for
open objectives
has remained elusive for more than 10 years
[
30
,
25
]
.

The generalisation of the theory of
monotone

universal graphs
to characterise memory, presented in
[
22
]
, offers a promising tool to establish tight upper bounds on memory requirements, which could be valuable to overcome impediments in the advancement of the study of memory for
\omega
-regular objectives
.

9.3
Minimisation and canonisation of parity automata

For the proof of Theorem
23
(Section
5.2
), we have introduced new notions concerning congruences for parity automata, as well as different transformations of automata.
This transformations exhibit a flavour similar to what one might expect from minimisation algorithms, as their main purpose is to remove redundant states from automata.
We believe that this techniques will be valuable for the study of
\omega
-automata in other contexts, as they allow for a fine analysis of the structure of the automata.

Also, a key ingredient in our proof is the use of
history-deterministic
automata, in particular, a generalisation of the minimisation algorithm for
history-deterministic

coBüchi automata
introduced by Abu Radi and Kupferman
[
1
]
. We see this fact as further evidence that
history-deterministic
automata provide canonicity properties.

In fact, we can derive actual concrete statements about the minimisation of automata from our results:

Proposition 140
.

Deterministic (resp.
history-deterministic
) parity automata
recognising

bipositional
languages can be minimised in polynomial time.

Proof.

A necessary condition for a language
L
to be
bipositional
is that it must be recognised by a
parity automaton on top
of the
automaton of residuals
(Theorem
116
). It turns out that such an automaton can be computed in polynomial time.
∎

Proposition 141
.

Deterministic (resp.
history-deterministic
)
Büchi
and
coBüchi automata

recognising

positional
languages can be minimised in polynomial time.

Proof.

In the case of
Büchi automata
, a
positional
language can be
recognised
by the
automaton of residuals
(Propositions
49
), which is necessary minimal amongst
history-deterministic
automata.

In the case of
coBüchi automata
, we obtained that the minimal
history-deterministic
automaton of Abu Radi and Kupferman, computable in polynomial time, can be taken
deterministic
for
positional
languages (Section
4.4
).∎

We conjecture that our methods may lead to similar results in the more general case of
parity automata
, and that minimal automata for
positional
languages can be obtained just by merging states of
signature automata
.

Conjecture 142
.

Deterministic
and
history-deterministic

parity automata

recognising

positional
languages can be minimised in polynomial time.
Moreover,
history-deterministic

parity automata
for this class of languages are not more succinct than
deterministic
ones.

Appendix A
Full proofs for Section
5.2

In this Appendix, we include full proofs for all the propositions and lemmas appearing in Section
5.2
.
In order to be able to tackle these proofs and formalise them in the simplest and cleanest possible way, we first introduce some technical artillery that will come in handy to deal with the structure of layered total preorders of
signature automata
.
We begin by introducing
nice transformations
of automata equipped with a
priority-faithful
relation in Section
A.1
.
Then, in Section
A.2
we give the full details of the induction constructing a
structured signature automaton
for a
positional
language.

A.1
Nice transformations of automata

To recursively build a
structured signature automaton
, we will apply a sequence of transformations to a given
d
-signature automaton

\mathcal{A}
, by removing states and adding or redirecting edges in such a way that relations
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
are preserved in a strong sense formalised in this section.
Before presenting the proofs of the results from Section
5.2
, we introduce some notations and prove technical lemmas that will come in handy to reason about (
structured
)
signature automata
.

{globalHyp*}

We recall that automata are assumed to be
complete
and
semantically deterministic
.

Automata with a common subautomaton

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a
semantically deterministic
automaton with states
Q_{\mathcal{A}}
, and let
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{\mathcal{A}}}
be the
congruence
given by the equality of
residuals
. We note that if
\mathcal{B}
is an automaton with states
Q_{\mathcal{B}}\subseteq Q_{\mathcal{A}}
, relation
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{\mathcal{A}}}
induces an equivalent relation over
Q_{\mathcal{B}}
(which, in general, is not a
congruence
nor coincides with the equality of
residuals
of
\mathcal{B}
).

Lemma 143

(Automata preserving the structure of residuals)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a
semantically deterministic

parity automaton
with states
Q_{\mathcal{A}}
and let
\mathcal{B}
be a
parity automaton
with states
Q_{\mathcal{B}}\subseteq Q_{\mathcal{A}}
. Assume that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{\mathcal{A}}}
is a
congruence
over
\mathcal{B}
and that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$\mathcal{B}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{{\scriptsize$\sim_{\mathcal{A}}$}}\right.}}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{{\scriptsize$\sim_{\mathcal{A}}$}}\right.}}
. Let
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be a
subautomaton
of both
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
.
If a word
w\in\Sigma^{\omega}
admits an
accepting run
in
\mathcal{B}
that eventually remains in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
, then
w
is also
accepted by

\mathcal{A}
.

Proof.

Let

q_{0}\xrightarrow{w_{0}}q_{1}\xrightarrow{w_{1}}q_{2}\xrightarrow{w_{2}}\dots\xrightarrow{w_{k-1}}q_{k}\xrightarrow{w_{k}}q_{k+1}\xrightarrow{w_{k+1}}\dots

be an
accepting run
over
w
in
\mathcal{B}
such that the suffix from
q_{k}
is contained in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
(meaning that both the states and the transitions used are part of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
).
We consider the
projection
of the prefix of size
k
of the run in the
quotient automaton

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{B}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\sim_{\mathcal{A}}$}}\right.}}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\sim_{\mathcal{A}}$}}\right.}}
. By Lemma
16
, there is a
run over

w_{0}\dots w_{k-1}
in
\mathcal{A}
,
p_{0}\xrightarrow{w_{0}}p_{1}\xrightarrow{w_{1}}\dots p_{k}
whose
projection
over the
quotient automaton
coincides with the previous one. Therefore,
p_{k}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{\mathcal{A}}}q_{k}
, that is,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}_{p_{k}}})}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}_{q_{k}}})}
. Since
w_{k+1}w_{k+2}\dots
admits an
accepting run
from
q_{k}
in
\mathcal{A}
, it also admits an
accepting run
from
p_{k}
, and
w
is
accepted
by
\mathcal{A}
.
∎

Nice transformations of automata

For
x\in\mathbb{N}
, we denote by
\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}{\left.\kern-1.2pt\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\vphantom{\big|}}{}{}{}\right|_{{\geq}x}}}
the
subautomaton
of
\mathcal{A}
induced by the set of transitions using a priority
\geq x
.

Definition 144

(Nice transformation at level
x
)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a
semantically deterministic

parity automaton
over
\Sigma
with states
Q
, let
x
be a
priority
, and let
\sim
be a
[0,x-1]
-faithful congruence
over
\mathcal{A}
.
Let
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be a
parity automaton
over
\Sigma
with states
Q^{\prime}\subseteq Q
. We denote
\sim
the induced relation over
Q^{\prime}
.
We say that
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a
\sim
-nice transformation of
\mathcal{A}
at level
x
if:

•

\sim
is a
[0,x-1]
-faithful congruence
over
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{{\scriptsize$\begin{matrix}[l]\phantom{.}\\[-2.56073pt]
{\sim}\\[-0.56905pt]
\hskip-4.55244pt{{{{{\leq}x-1}}}}\end{matrix}$}}\right.}}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{{\scriptsize$\begin{matrix}[l]\phantom{.}\\[-2.56073pt]
{\sim}\\[-0.56905pt]
\hskip-4.55244pt{{{{{\leq}x-1}}}}\end{matrix}$}}\right.}}
,

•

\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{\mathcal{A}}}
is a
congruence
over
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{{\scriptsize$\sim_{\mathcal{A}}$}}\right.}}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.02228pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.02228pt}{{\scriptsize$\sim_{\mathcal{A}}$}}\right.}}
, and

•

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\left.\kern-1.2pt\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\mathchoice{\vphantom{\big|}}{}{}{}\right|_{{\geq}x+1}}}
coincides with the
subautomaton
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\left.\kern-1.2pt\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\vphantom{\big|}}{}{}{}\right|_{{\geq}x+1}}}
induced by the states in
Q^{\prime}
.

Intuitively, if
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a
nice transformation
of
\mathcal{A}
at level
x
, it means that the only relevant modifications applied to
\mathcal{A}
concern
x
-transitions
. The structure of the
quotient automaton
for priorities
{<}x
is left unchanged, and so is the acceptance of runs that eventually only produce priorities
{>}x
.

Remark 145
.

We note that if
\sim
is an equivalence relation that
refines

\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{\mathcal{A}}}
, then the second item of Definition
144
is implied by the first one. This is in particular the case if
\sim
is an equivalent relation
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
of a
d
-signature automaton
, for
0\leq x\leq d
.

Lemma 147
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a
\varepsilon
-completion
that admits a
[0,x]
-faithful congruence

\sim
. If a word
w\in\Sigma^{\omega}
admits a run such that the minimal priority produced infinitely often is
y\leq x
, then the minimal priority produced infinitely often by any
run over
w
is
y
. In particular, if
y
is odd,
w

is rejected with priority

y
.

Proof.

Let
q_{0}\xrightarrow{w_{1}:y_{1}}q_{1}\xrightarrow{w_{2}:y_{2}}\dots
and
q_{0}^{\prime}=q_{0}\xrightarrow{w_{1}:y_{1}^{\prime}}q_{1}^{\prime}\xrightarrow{w_{2}:y_{2}^{\prime}}\dots
be two runs over the same word in
\mathcal{A}
(
q_{0}=q_{0}^{\prime}
being the
initial state
of
\mathcal{A}
). Since
\sim
is a congruence, we obtain by induction that
q_{i}\sim q_{i}^{\prime}
for every
i
. Moreover, as, for
y\leq x
,
y
-transitions
act uniformly
over
\sim
-classes, each time that
y_{i}\leq x
, we have that
y_{i}^{\prime}=x_{i}
.
∎

Lemma 148

(Nice transformations preserve acceptance of most words)
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
be a
semantically deterministic

parity automaton
equipped with a
[0,x-1]
-faithful congruence

\sim
.
Let
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be a
\sim
-nice transformation of
\mathcal{A}
at level
x
. We have:

•

A word
w\in\Sigma^{\omega}
can be
accepted with an even priority

y<x
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
if and only if
w
can be
accepted with priority

y
in
\mathcal{A}
.

•

A word
w\in\Sigma^{\omega}
is
rejected with an odd priority

y<x
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
if and only if
w
is
rejected with priority

y
in
\mathcal{A}
.

•

If a word
w\in\Sigma^{\omega}
can be
accepted with an even priority

y>x
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
, then it is
accepted by

\mathcal{A}
.

If moreover
\mathcal{A}
is
homogeneous
and
deterministic over
transitions using priorities
>x
, we have:

•

If there is a
rejecting
run over
w\in\Sigma^{\omega}
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
producing as minimal priority
y>x
, then
w
is
rejected
by
\mathcal{A}
.

Proof.

Let
w\in\Sigma^{\omega}
be a word
accepted with a priority

y<x
in
\mathcal{A}
(resp.
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
). Then, by Lemma
76
,
w
is
accepted by
the
quotient automaton

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\begin{matrix}[l]\phantom{.}\\[-2.56073pt]
{\sim}\\[-0.56905pt]
\hskip-4.55244pt{{{{{\leq}x-1}}}}\end{matrix}$}}\right.}}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\begin{matrix}[l]\phantom{.}\\[-2.56073pt]
{\sim}\\[-0.56905pt]
\hskip-4.55244pt{{{{{\leq}x-1}}}}\end{matrix}$}}\right.}}
. Again by Lemma
76
,
w
is
accepted by

\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
(resp.
\mathcal{A}
). The second item is obtained using the same argument, combined with Lemma
147
.

The third item is directly implied by Lemma
143
, as
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\left.\kern-1.2pt\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\mathchoice{\vphantom{\big|}}{}{}{}\right|_{{\geq}x+1}}}
is a
subautomaton
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\left.\kern-1.2pt\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\vphantom{\big|}}{}{}{}\right|_{{\geq}x+1}}}
.

A.2.1

Lemma 151

(Total order of residual classes)
.

Let
W\subseteq\Sigma^{\omega}
be an
\omega
-regular
objective that is
positional
over finite,
\varepsilon
-free

Eve-games
. Then,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Res}(W)}
is totally ordered by inclusion.

Proof.

The proof is almost identical to that of Lemma
33
.
We show the contrapositive.
Assume that
W
has two incomparable
residuals
,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{1}}^{-1}W

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}u_{2}}^{-1}W

We consider first the case
u_{1}\neq\varepsilon
and
u_{2}\neq\varepsilon

Take

We have

u_{1}w_{2}\notin W
,

u_{2}w_{1}\notin W

u_{2}w_{2}\in W
.

A.2.2
Safe centrality and relation
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}
. Proof of Lemma
87

In this paragraph we give a proof of Lemma
87
. We assume that

is an even priority and
\mathcal{A}

See
87

Hypothesis.

During the proof, we will lose the

of

. However, in all the subsection we will maintain the three first required properties. In the statements of all lemmas,
\mathcal{A}
will stand for an

-structured signature

•

Saturation.

We say that an automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is
(x-1)
-saturated
if for every state
q
and letter
a\in\Sigma
, if a transition
q\xrightarrow{a:x-1}p
exists in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
, then
q\xrightarrow{a:x-1}p^{\prime}
appears in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
for all
p^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}p
.
12
12

12

We note that this definition slightly differs from the definition of
1
-saturation
used in the warm-up (Section
4.4
). In particular, the definition of the warm-up does not preserve
homogeneity
. We allow ourselves these small disagreements of definitions for the sake of clarity in the presentation in each respective subsection.

The
(x-1)
-saturation
of
\mathcal{A}
is the automaton obtained by adding all those transitions.

Remark 152
.

The
(x-1)
-saturation
of
\mathcal{A}
is
homogeneous
and
deterministic over
transitions with
priority
different from
x-1
.

The following lemma states that
(x-1)
-saturation
is a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
-nice transformation at level
x-1
, so Lemmas
148
and
146
can be applied. We recall that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}

refines

\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{\mathcal{A}}}
, so congruence of
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{\mathcal{A}}}
is implied by that of
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
.

Lemma 154
.

The
(x-1)
-saturation
of
\mathcal{A}
is a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
-nice transformation of
\mathcal{A}
at level
x-1
.

Proof.

Let
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be the
(x-1)
-saturation
of
\mathcal{A}
.
It is immediate that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\left.\kern-1.2pt\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\vphantom{\big|}}{}{}{}\right|_{{\geq}x}}}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\left.\kern-1.2pt\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\mathchoice{\vphantom{\big|}}{}{}{}\right|_{{\geq}x}}}
. Moreover, the restriction of
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
to transitions using priorities
\leq x-2
coincides, so for each
0\leq y\leq x-2
, relation
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
is a
congruence for

y
-transitions
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
(and therefore these transitions
act uniformly
by
determinism
). The
congruence for
transitions using priority
{>}(x-2)
is preserved as we have only added
(x-1)
-transitions that go to the same
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
-class.
As
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}

refines

\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{\mathcal{A}}}
, the latter relation is also a
congruence
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\sim_{\mathcal{A}}$}}\right.}}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\sim_{\mathcal{A}}$}}\right.}}
.
∎

Lemma 155
.

The
(x-1)
-saturation
of
\mathcal{A}

recognises

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}
. Moreover, it is
history-deterministic
,
homogeneous
and
deterministic over transitions
using
priorities
different from
x-1
.

Proof.

Let
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be the
(x-1)
-saturation
of
\mathcal{A}
. We have already noted that it is
homogeneous
and
deterministic over transitions
using
priority
different from
x-1
(Remark
152
).
If
w\in\Sigma^{\omega}
is
accepted by

\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
(resp. by
\mathcal{A}
), it is either
accepted with
an even priority
y<x-1
or
y>x-1
. In the first case, since
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
-nice transformation at level
x-1
, Lemma
148
allows us to conclude. In the second case, it suffices to apply Lemma
143
.

History-determinism
of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is clear: one can use a
resolver
for
\mathcal{A}
.
∎

Redundant safe components.

From now on, we suppose that
\mathcal{A}
is
(x-1)
-saturated
.

We say that a
({<}x)
-safe component

S
of
\mathcal{A}
is
redundant
if there is
q\in S
and
q^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}q
,
q^{\prime}\notin S
, such that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(q)\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(q^{\prime})
. We note that, by
normality
of
\mathcal{A}
, there are no
({\geq}x)
-transitions
entering in
S
; that is, there are no transitions
p\xrightarrow{a:\geq x}q
with
p\notin S
and
q\in S
.

Remark 156
.

Automaton
\mathcal{A}
is
({<}x)
-safe centralised
if and only if it does not contain any
redundant

({<}x)
-safe component
.

Lemma 157
.

If
\mathcal{A}
contains some
redundant

({<}x)
-safe component
, we can find one of them in polynomial time.

Proof.

The computation of the
({<}x)
-safe components
of
\mathcal{A}
can be done by simply a decomposition in
SCC
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\left.\kern-1.2pt\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\vphantom{\big|}}{}{}{}\right|_{{\geq}x}}}
.
For each pair of states
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}q^{\prime}
in different
({<}x)
-safe components
we just need to check the inclusion
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(q)\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(q^{\prime})
, which can be done in polynomial time.
∎

Lemma 158

Removing redundant safe components.

For now on, fix
S
to be a
redundant

({<}x)
-safe component
of
\mathcal{A}
, and
S^{\prime}
a different
({<}x)
-safe component
as in the previous lemma.
For each
q\in S
, we let
\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}f}(q)\in S^{\prime}
such that
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(q)
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(q)\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(q))
.
We extend
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}
to all of
Q
by setting it to be the identity over
Q\setminus S
.

We define the automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
as follows:

•

The set of states is
Q^{\prime}=Q\setminus S
.

•

The
initial state
is
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(q_{\mathsf{init}})
.

•

For each
p\in Q^{\prime}
, if
p\xrightarrow{a:y}q
is a transition in
\mathcal{A}
, we let
p\xrightarrow{a:y}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(q)
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

We note that, if
q\notin S
, all transitions
p\xrightarrow{a:y}q
in
\mathcal{A}
are left unchanged. In particular, the
({\geq}x)
-transitions
of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
are the restriction of those appearing in
\mathcal{A}
,
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is
(x-1)
-saturated
, and
({<}x)
-transitions
in
\mathcal{A}
not entering in
S
appear in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
too.
We say that transitions
p\xrightarrow{a:y}q
of
\mathcal{A}
such that
q\in S
have been
redirected in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

Lemma 159
.

Automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
-nice transformation of
\mathcal{A}
at level
x-1
.

Proof.

We have that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\left.\kern-1.2pt\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\mathchoice{\vphantom{\big|}}{}{}{}\right|_{{\geq}x}}}
is the
subautomaton
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\left.\kern-1.2pt\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\vphantom{\big|}}{}{}{}\right|_{{\geq}x}}}
induced by states in
Q^{\prime}
. We show that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
is
[0,x-2]
-faithful
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.
Transitions that have not been
redirected
satisfy the congruence requirements, as they satisfy them in
\mathcal{A}
.
Let
p\xrightarrow{a:y}q
and
p^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:y^{\prime}}q_{0}^{\prime}
be two transitions in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
such that
y\leq x-2
,
p\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}p^{\prime}
and such that the second transition has been redirected from
p^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:y^{\prime}}q^{\prime}
(the first transition is possibly a redirected one too).
By the congruence property in
\mathcal{A}
, we have that
y^{\prime}=y
and
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}q^{\prime}
. Since
q^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}q_{0}^{\prime}
, we conclude by transitivity.
The equality
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\begin{matrix}[l]\phantom{.}\\[-2.56073pt]
{\sim_{x-2}}\\[-0.56905pt]
\hskip-4.55244pt{{{{{\leq}x-1}}}}\end{matrix}$}}\right.}}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\begin{matrix}[l]\phantom{.}\\[-2.56073pt]
{\sim_{x-2}}\\[-0.56905pt]
\hskip-4.55244pt{{{{{\leq}x-1}}}}\end{matrix}$}}\right.}}
simply follows from the fact that
redirected
transitions have been defined preserving the
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
-classes.

As
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}

refines

\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{\mathcal{A}}}
, the latter relation is also a
congruence
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\sim_{\mathcal{A}}$}}\right.}}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\sim_{\mathcal{A}}$}}\right.}}
.
∎

Lemma 160

(Correctness of the removal of redundant components)
.

For every state
q^{\prime}\in Q^{\prime}
, we have
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}^{\prime}_{q^{\prime}}})}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}_{q^{\prime}}})}
.
In particular, these automata are
equivalent
.
Moreover, automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is
deterministic over
transitions with
priority
different from
x-1
,
homogeneous
and
history-deterministic
.

Proof.

The fact that
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is
deterministic over
transitions with
priority
different from
x-1
and
homogeneous
is immediate from its definition.
We show the equality of languages for the
initial state
. The proof is identical for a different state.

The inclusion
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})}\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}
directly follows from Lemma
148
.

We describe a
sound resolver
witnessing
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})}
and
history-determinism
. Take a
sound resolver

\mathsf{r}
in
\mathcal{A}
, let
w\in\Sigma^{\omega}
, and write

\rho=p_{0}\xrightarrow{w_{0}}p_{1}\xrightarrow{w_{1}}\dots

for the run in
\mathcal{A}

induced by

\mathsf{r}
over
w
.
We will build a
resolver

\mathsf{r}^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
satisfying the property that the
run induced over
w
,
\rho^{\prime}=p^{\prime}_{0}\xrightarrow{w_{0}}p^{\prime}_{1}\xrightarrow{w_{1}}\dots
is in one of the following (non-excluding) cases:

a)

produces priorities
<x-1
infinitely often,

b)

eventually produces only priorities
\geq x
,

c)

p_{i}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}p^{\prime}_{i}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p_{i})\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p_{i}^{\prime})
for every
i
sufficiently large.

Claim 161
.

A
resolver

\mathsf{r}^{\prime}
satisfying the property above accepts all words in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}
.

{claimproof}

Suppose that
w\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}
, that is, the run
\rho

induced by

\mathsf{r}
is
accepting
. Let
\rho^{\prime}
be the
run induced over
w
by
\mathsf{r}^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
. We distinguish two cases, according to the priorities produced by the run
\rho
in
\mathcal{A}
:

If
\rho
produces priorities
<x-1
infinitely often. Then Lemma
148
allows us to conclude.

If
\rho
eventually only produces priorities
\geq x-1
.
Then, the two first items of Lemma
148
tells us that
\rho^{\prime}
eventually only produces priorities
\geq x-1
too (so we are not in Case
a
).
We show that
\rho^{\prime}
eventually only produces priorities
>x-1
; the last item of Lemma
148
allows us to conclude (we recall that
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
-nice transformation at level
x-1
).
If we are in Case
b
, this property is trivially satisfied. Suppose that we are in Case
c
, and let
k>0
be such that the suffix of
\rho
from
q_{k}
only produces priorities
\geq x
and such that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p_{i})\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p_{i}^{\prime})
for
i\geq k
. Therefore, there is a
run over
w_{k}w_{k+1}\dots
from
p_{k}^{\prime}
producing exclusively priorities
\geq x
. By
determinism over transitions
with priority
\geq x
, this run is the one
induced by

\mathsf{r}^{\prime}
.

We finally show how to construct a
resolver
with this property.
We let
p^{\prime}_{0}=f(p_{0})
, and assume
\rho^{\prime}
constructed up to
p^{\prime}_{i}
satisfying that
p^{\prime}_{i}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}p_{i}
.

If there is a transition
p^{\prime}_{i}\xrightarrow{w_{i}:y}p^{\prime}_{i+1}
with
y\neq x-1
, then we take this one (there is no other option), which satisfies
p_{i+1}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}p_{i+1}^{\prime}
by Lemma
159
.
Moreover, if
y\geq x
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p_{i})\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p_{i}^{\prime})
, then
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p_{i+1})\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p_{i+1}^{\prime})
by Lemma
82
.
If there is a transition
p^{\prime}_{i}\xrightarrow{w_{i}:x-1}
, we take
p_{i+1}^{\prime}=f(p_{i+1})
(this transition exists in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
by
x-1
-saturation
, as
p^{\prime}_{i}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}p_{i}
).

We show that this
resolver
satisfies the desired property. Suppose that we are not in the two first cases, that is,
\rho^{\prime}
eventually only produces priorities
\geq x-1
, and it produces priority
x-1
infinitely often. Take a suffix
p^{\prime}_{k}\xrightarrow{w_{k}:y_{k}}p^{\prime}_{k+1}\xrightarrow{w_{k+1}:y_{k+1}}\dots
of
\rho^{\prime}
such that no priority
<x-1
is produced and such that
y_{k}=x-1
. Then, by definition of the transitions using
x-1
chosen by the
resolver
,
p_{k+1}^{\prime}=f(p_{k+1})
, so
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p_{k+1})\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}_{<x}(p_{k+1}^{\prime})
. We conclude by induction, as transitions taken by the resolver using priorities
\geq x-1
preserve the inclusion of
({<}x)
-safe languages
.
∎

Transformation preserves being a structured signature automaton.

To be able to finish the proof of Lemma
87
, we just need to show that
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a
(x-2)
-structured signature automaton
. We give some technical lemmas that will help us show this.

.

Item
1
.

By Lemma
160
, the residuals in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
correspond to those in
\mathcal{A}
, so
preorder

\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{0}}
correspond to their inclusion in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
too.

Item
2
.

By the previous remarks, for all
y
, the
({<}y)
-safe components
of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
are obtaining by taking the intersection with those in
\mathcal{A}
. Therefore, odd preorders
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{y-1}}
correspond to the order of
({<}y)
-safe components
on
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

Item
3
.

As
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
-nice transformation at level
x-1
, for every
y<x-1
and state
q^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}^{\mathcal{A}^{\prime}}_{<y}(q^{\prime})={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}^{\mathcal{A}}_{<y}(q^{\prime})
. Therefore, the preorders at even levels
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{y}}
correspond to the inclusion of safe languages in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
, as they do in
\mathcal{A}
.

Item
4
.

Let
q
and
q^{\prime}
be two states in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
such that
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{y}}q^{\prime}
, for
y\leq x-2
even, and let
q\xrightarrow{a:y^{\prime}}p
for
y^{\prime}\leq y
and
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:z}p^{\prime}
.
As
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a
nice transformation
,
y^{\prime}=z
.
If the first of these transitions is not a
redirected
one, then, by
strong congruence
of
{\leq}(x-2)
-priorities in
\mathcal{A}
, neither is the second one, and
p=p^{\prime}
.
Assume that these transitions have been
redirected
from,
q\xrightarrow{a:y^{\prime}}p_{1}
and
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:y^{\prime}}p^{\prime}_{1}
. Then, as Item
4
is satisfied in
\mathcal{A}
,
p_{1}=p^{\prime}_{1}
, so
p={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(p_{1})={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(p_{1}^{\prime})=p^{\prime}
.

Item
5
.

Directly follows from Lemma
163
and the fact that
\mathcal{A}
satisfies this property.

Item
6
.

Follows from the fact that if
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\nsim}_{y-1}}p
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
, then
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\nsim}_{y-1}}p
in
\mathcal{A}
; and the equality
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}^{\mathcal{A}^{\prime}}_{<y}(q)={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}^{\mathcal{A}}_{<y}(q)
.∎

Obtaining Lemma
87
.

We have all the necessary elements to deduce Lemma
87
. Using Lemma
157
, we can decide whether
\mathcal{A}
contains a
redundant

({<}x)
-safe component
in polynomial time.
If it contains none,
\mathcal{A}
is already
({<}x)
-safe centralised
.
While we can find
redundant
safe components, we remove them applying the transformation described above. This transformation can clearly be done in polynomial time, and by Lemmas
160
and
164
, the obtained automaton
recognises
the correct language and preserves all the hypothesis assumed in the induction.

A.2.3
Existence of uniform words and synchronising separating runs

We now provide proofs for Lemmas
89
and
90
.
In Section

, we derived totality of the order
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
in each
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}
-component from these lemmas (c.f. Lemma

).

homogeneous

uniformly.

89

Resolvers implemented by finite memories.

For the upcoming proofs, we need to introduced the notion of memories for
resolvers
.
Let
\mathcal{A}=(Q,\Sigma,q_{\mathsf{init}},\Delta,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{p}})
be a
non-deterministic automaton
. A
memory structure
for
\mathcal{A}
is a tuple
(M,m_{\mathsf{init}},\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}\mu},{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sigma})
, where
M
is a set of memory states,
m_{\mathsf{init}}\in M
is an initial state,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mu}:M\times\Delta\to M
is an
update function
and
\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}\sigma}\colon Q\times M\times\Sigma\to\Delta
.
It
implements
a
resolver

\mathsf{r}
if for all
a\in\Sigma
,
\mathsf{r}(\varepsilon,a)={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sigma}(q_{\mathsf{init}},m_{\mathsf{init}},a)
and for all
\rho\in\Delta^{+}
ending in
p
,
\mathsf{r}(\rho,a)={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sigma}(p,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mu}(m_{\mathsf{init}},\rho),a)
.

A.2.4
Re-determinisation

We give the proof of Lemma
92
, that is, we show that we can obtain an
equivalent

deterministic
automaton from
\mathcal{A}
while preserving all the obtained structure of
total preorders
satisfying the conditions of a
structured signature automaton
.

Hypothesis.

We assume that
\mathcal{A}
is a
parity automaton

recognising

W
with
nested total preorders
defined up to
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
such that:

•

it is a
(x-2)
-structured signature automaton
,

•

preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x-1}}
satisfies properties from Items
2
and
6
from the definition of a
structured signature automaton
,

•

preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
satisfies the property from Item
3
from the definition of a
structured signature automaton
,

•

it is
deterministic over
transitions with priorities different from
x-1
,

•

it is
homogeneous
, and

•

it is
history-deterministic
.

Obtaining a deterministic automaton.

See
92

An intuitive idea for the construction of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
was given in Section
5.2
. We formalise it and prove its correctness now.

Automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is obtained by keeping all the structure of
\mathcal{A}
, except for
(x-1)
-transitions; for each state
q
and letter
a
such that some transition
q\xrightarrow{a:x-1}p
appears in
\mathcal{A}
, we will redefine this transition as
q\xrightarrow{a:x-1}p^{\prime}
for some
p^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}p
as determined next.

For each
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}
-class
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x-1}}
of
\mathcal{A}
, we pick a state in the class that is maximal for
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
. We let
\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}f}(q)
be that state. That is, for two states
q_{1}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}q_{2}
:

•

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(q_{1})={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(q_{2})
,

•

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(q_{1})\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q_{1}]_{x-1}}
, and

•

q_{1}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(q_{1})
.

We recall that we have a total order over the
{<}x
-safe components
of
\mathcal{A}
given by
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{1},{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{2},\dots,{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{k_{x}}
.
Let
q\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{i}
and
a\in\Sigma
such that
q\xrightarrow{a:x-1}p
appears in
\mathcal{A}
.
If it exists, we let
\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}i}_{\mathsf{next}}
be the maximal
0\leq i_{\mathsf{next}}<i
such that there is some
p^{\prime}\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[p]_{x-2}}
,
p^{\prime}\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{i_{\mathsf{next}}}
. If index
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}i}_{\mathsf{next}}
is not defined, we let it be the maximal index
i\leq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}i}_{\mathsf{next}}\leq k_{x}
with the previous property.
We fix a state
p_{q,a}\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}i}_{\mathsf{next}}}
with
p_{q,a}\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[p]_{x-2}}
.
We let the
a
-transition
from
q
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be
q\xrightarrow{a:x-1}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(p_{q,a})
.
This completes the description of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
. It is indeed
deterministic
, as
\mathcal{A}
is
homogeneous
and
deterministic over
transitions with priorities different from
x-1
.

We can find a maximal state
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(q)
for
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
in the class
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x-1}}
in polynomial time, as the comparison of
{<}x
-safe languages
can be done in polynomial time (Lemma
107
).
Therefore, automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
can be built in polynomial time.

Lemma 166
.

Automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
-nice transformation of
\mathcal{A}
at level
x-1
.

Proof.

This is clear, as the restriction of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
to transitions using a
priority
different from
(x-1)
coincides with that of
\mathcal{A}
, and every transition
q\xrightarrow{a:x-1}p^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
comes from a transition
q\xrightarrow{a:x-1}p
in
\mathcal{A}
with
p\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}p^{\prime}
.
∎

Lemma 167
.

For every state
q\in Q
, we have
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}^{\prime}_{q}})}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}_{q}})}
.
In particular, automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}

recognises
the language
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}

Proof.

For simplicity, we give the proof just for the initial state; the proof being identical for any other state.

\mathcal{A}

is a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
-nice transformation of
\mathcal{A}
at level
x-1
.

\mathcal{A}

{customclaim}

167
.1
Eventually,
i_{j}=i_{\mathcal{A}}
.

{claimproof}
Consider a transition
q_{k_{j}}^{\prime}\xrightarrow{w_{k_{j}}:x-1}q_{k_{j}+1}^{\prime}
, and suppose first that
i_{\mathcal{A}}<i_{j-1}
.
We claim that
i_{\mathcal{A}}\leq i_{j}<i_{j-1}
. This would end the proof, as we obtain a strictly decreasing sequence of indices bounded by
i_{\mathcal{A}}
.
In order to determine
i_{j}
, we need to look at the definition of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}i}_{\mathsf{next}}
. As
q_{k}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}q_{k}^{\prime}
for all
k
, there are always states in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q_{k_{j}+1}^{\prime}]_{x-2}}
in some
{<}x
-safe components
with an index
i_{\mathcal{A}}\leq i<i_{j-1}
.
Thus, we obtain the desired result by definition of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}i}_{\mathsf{next}}
.

If
i_{j-1}\leq i_{\mathcal{A}}
, by definition of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}i}_{\mathsf{next}}
, there is be a sequence of decreasing indices
i_{j-1}>i_{j}>i_{j+1}>\dots
until no
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
-equivalent state appears in a strictly smaller safe component.
By the same argument as before, there is always a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
-equivalent state in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}S}^{{<}x}_{i_{\mathcal{A}}}
, so eventually
i_{\mathcal{A}}\leq i_{j^{\prime}}
, and either this is an equality, or we reduce to the previous case.

Let
j
be the first position such that
i_{j}=i_{\mathcal{A}}
, and consider transitions
q_{k_{j}}\xrightarrow{w_{k_{j}}:\geq x}q_{k_{j}+1}
and
q_{k_{j}}^{\prime}\xrightarrow{w_{k_{j}}:x-1}q_{k_{j}+1}^{\prime}
in
\rho
and
\rho^{\prime}
, respectively.
By definition of
x-1
-transitions
of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
, the state we go to in
\rho^{\prime}
is
q_{k_{j}+1}^{\prime}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(q_{k_{j}+1})
.
As we have chosen
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(q_{k_{j}+1})
maximal in its
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}
-class, we have
q_{k_{j}+1}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}q_{k_{j}+1}^{\prime}
, so we have the inclusion of
{<}x
-safe languages
between these states.
Therefore, if there is a
{<}x
-safe run
over
w^{\prime}
from
q_{k_{j}+1}
in
\mathcal{A}
, there is also such a
safe run
over
w^{\prime}
from
q_{k_{j}+1}^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.
This contradicts the fact that the run
\rho^{\prime}
produces priority
x-1
infinitely often, while the run
\rho
is
{<}x
-safe
from
q_{k_{j}+1}
, concluding the proof. ∎

To finish the proof of Lemma
92
, we just need to show that
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
preserves all the properties of the preorders induced by
\mathcal{A}
.
As in the previous section, to obtain
normality
of the automaton and Item
5
, we rely on a technical lemma that tells us that we can connect states in the same
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
-component as desired.

Lemma 168
.

Let
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}p
be two different states in
Q
. There is a word

Lemma 170
.

Automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
, with the preorders
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{0}},\dots,\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
inherited from
\mathcal{A}
satisfies:

•

it is a
(x-2)
-structured signature automaton
,

•

preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x-1}}
satisfies properties from Items
2
and
6
from the definition of a
structured signature automaton
, and

•

preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
satisfies the property from Item
3
and, for priorities
y<x
, also that from Item
4
.

Proof.

We start verifying the properties for the preorders
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x-1}}
and
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
.
We note that the
{<}x
-safe components
of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
exactly correspond to those in
\mathcal{A}
, and that for every
q\in Q
,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}^{\mathcal{A}}_{<x}(q)={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathsf{Safe}}^{\mathcal{A}^{\prime}}_{<x}(q)
. The fact that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x-1}}
satisfies Items
2
and
6
, and that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
satisfies Item
3
follows immediately.
We check that relation
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
satisfies Item
4
for priorities
y<x
. For
y\leq x-2
, this follows from the fact that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
refines
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
, and the latter relation satisfies Item
4
. For
y=x-1
, if
q\xrightarrow{a:x-1}p
and
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:x-1}p^{\prime}
, with
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}q^{\prime}
, by definition of the
x-1
-transitions
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
,
p={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(p)={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(p^{\prime})=p^{\prime}
.

Checking that
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a
(x-2)
-structured signature automaton
poses no difficulty. It can be done in an analogous way as it was done in the proof of Lemma
164
; by applying Lemma
169
to obtain
normality
of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
and property from Item
5
. ∎

A.2.5
Uniformity of
x
-transitions over
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-classes

We finally show how to transform
\mathcal{A}
into an
equivalent
automaton that is either
x
-structured signature
, or strictly smaller. The techniques presented here generalise those applying to Büchi automata appearing in Section
4.3
of the warm-up.

Hypothesis.

In all this subsection we suppose that
\mathcal{A}
is
deterministic

parity automaton

recognising

W
with
nested total preorders
defined up to
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
such that:

•

it is a
(x-2)
-structured signature automaton
,

•

preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x-1}}
satisfies properties from Items
2
and
6
from the definition of a
structured signature automaton
, and

•

preorder
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
is a
congruence
and satisfies the property from Item
3
and, for priorities
y<x
, also that from Item
4
.

Our objective is to prove, under this list of hypothesis, that we can either obtain an
equivalent

deterministic

x
-structured signature automaton
, or reduce the number of states of
\mathcal{A}
.

See
93

We remark that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
already satisfies most desired properties of
monotonicity
; only the
uniformity for

x
-transitions is missing.

Lemma 171
.

The relation
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
is a
[0,x-1]
-faithful congruence
. Moreover, over each
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}
-class, transitions using priorities
{\geq}x
are
monotone for

\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
.

Proof.

The
[0,x-2]
-faithfulness
follows from the fact that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
refines
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-2}}
and
\mathcal{A}
is
(x-2)
-structured signature
.
The
uniformity
of
(x-1)
-transitions over
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-classes is given by the fact that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-equivalent states have the same
{<}x
-safe language
, combined with the
uniformity
of
{<}(x-1)
-transitions.

The fact that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
is a
congruence for

(x-1)
-transitions
follows from Item
4
of the definition of a
structured signature automaton
(we recall that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
satisfies this property by hypothesis).
The
congruence for

{\geq}x
-transitions and the monotonicity of
{\geq}x
-transitions for
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
at each
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x-1}}
-class follow from the monotonicity of
{<}x
-safe languages
(Lemma
82
).
∎

We say that the automaton
\mathcal{A}
is
x
-polished
if all its
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-classes are
x
-polished
.

Remark 173
.

We remark that, as
x\geq 2
and we assume that the automaton
\mathcal{A}
is in
normal form
, all non-trivial
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-classes are
recurrent
: if a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-class is not trivial, there is a cycle visiting all the states of the class.
Therefore, we do not need to take care of
transient classes
(as it was the case in Lemma
53
from the warm-up).

Lemma 174
.

We can decide whether
\mathcal{A}
is
x
-polished
in polynomial time.

Proof.

As
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
is a
[0,x-1]
-faithful congruence
(Lemma
171
), we just need to check the first property for letters, which can be done in linear time in
|\Sigma||\mathcal{A}|
.

For the second property, we just need to check whether, for each
q\in Q
, the
subautomaton
induced by
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
and transitions with priority
{>}x
is strongly connected.
∎

Case 1:
\mathcal{A}
is already
x
-polished

Assume that
\mathcal{A}
is
x
-polished
. In this case, it is almost an
x
-structured signature automaton
. We just need to ensure that if
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}q^{\prime}
, two transitions
q\xrightarrow{a:x}p
and
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:x}p^{\prime}
go to a same state
p=p^{\prime}
.

We remark that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
already satisfies most desired properties of
monotonicity
; only the
uniformity for

x
-transitions is missing.

In order to obtain the
strong congruence
of
x
-transitions (Item
4
), we redirect some
x
-transitions of
\mathcal{A}
.
For each
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-class
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
, pick an arbitrary state
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(q)\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
. (Formally,
\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}f}\colon Q\to Q
such that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(q)={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(q^{\prime})
if
q\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}q^{\prime}
). We let
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
be the automaton obtained as follows:

•

The states of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
are the same than those in
\mathcal{A}
.

•

Transitions using priorities different from
x
are those in
\mathcal{A}
.

•

If
q\xrightarrow{a:x}p
, we let
q\xrightarrow{a:x}{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}f}(p)
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

It is immediate to check that
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-nice transformation of
\mathcal{A}
at level
x
. Moreover,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\left.\kern-1.2pt\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\vphantom{\big|}}{}{}{}\right|_{{\geq}x+1}}}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\left.\kern-1.2pt\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\mathchoice{\vphantom{\big|}}{}{}{}\right|_{{\geq}x+1}}}
. These remarks directly give:

Lemma 175
.

\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is
x
-polished
.

Lemma 177
.

Automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is
equivalent to

\mathcal{A}
, and it is an
x
-structured signature automaton
.

Proof.

The fact that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})}
follows easily using that
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-nice transformation of
\mathcal{A}
at level
x
and applying Lemma
148
.
Lemma
176
implies that
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is in
normal form
.
Verifying that
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is an
x
-structured signature automaton
is just a routine check, using that
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is
x
-polished
and Lemma
176
.
∎

Super words and super letters for local languages.

We recall some terminology introduced in the warm-up. Assume that
L
is a
prefix-independent
language.
We say that
u\in\Sigma^{+}
is a
super word
for
L
if, for every
w\in\Sigma^{\omega}
, if
w
contains
u
infinitely often as a factor, then
w\in L
.
If
s
is a letter, we say that it is a
super letter
.

For
q
a state and
x
an even priority, we let
\immediate\immediate\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}B}_{[q]_{x}}\subseteq{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[q]_{x}}
be the set of
super letters for

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{[q]_{x}}}
, and we write
\immediate{\color[rgb]{0.3438,0.0195,0.0273}N}_{[q]_{x}}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[q]_{x}}\setminus{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}B}_{[q]_{x}}
. We refer to
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}N}_{[q]_{x}}
as the set of
neutral letters
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[q]_{x}}
(for
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{[q]_{x}}}
).

∎

In particular, using previous lemma, we can detect the set of

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}B}_{[q]_{x}}
in polynomial time.

Super words of positional languages.

The use of the hypothesis of
positionality
of
W
for proving Lemma
93
resides in the next fundamental result.

Lemma 179

(Neutral letters do not form super words)
.

Let
w\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[q]_{x}}^{+}
be a
super word
for
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{[q]_{x}}}
. Then,
w
contains some
super letter
.

Proof.

If
w
is already a letter in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[q]_{x}}
, we are done. If not, let
w=w_{1}w_{2}
be any non-trivial decomposition into smaller words
w_{1},w_{2}\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[q]_{x}}^{+}
. We show that either
w_{1}
or
w_{2}
are
super words
for
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{[q]_{x}}}
. This allows us to finish the proof, as we can recursively chop
w
into strictly smaller
super words
until obtaining a
super letter
.

Suppose by contradiction that neither
w_{1}
or
w_{2}
are
super words
. Then, by Lemma
178

We consider the
game

\mathcal{G}
with
winning condition

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}_{q}})}
consisting in a vertex

with self loops
u_{1}w_{1}
and
u_{2}w_{2}
(see Figure
8
from the warm-up).

Eve
can
win
game
\mathcal{G}
, as alternating the two self loops she produces the word
(u_{1}w_{1}w_{2}u_{2})^{\omega}
, which belongs to
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}_{q}})}
since
w_{1}w_{2}
is a
super word
.
However,
positional strategies
in this game produce either
(w_{1}u_{1})^{\omega}
or
(w_{2}u_{2})^{\omega}
, both losing.
This contradicts the
positionality
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}_{q}})}
, and therefore, that of
W
(Lemma
149
).
∎

Polishing a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-class of
\mathcal{A}
.

We show how to
polish
the class
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
of
\mathcal{A}
. This process has the property that, either
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
is already
polished
, or the obtained automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
has strictly less states than
\mathcal{A}
, as desired.

Assume that the class
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
is not
x
-polished
.
Consider the restriction of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}}_{[q]_{x}}
to transitions labelled with
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}N}_{[q]_{x}}
, which we denote
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}}_{[q]_{x}}^{\prime}
. Take
S_{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}}
to be a
final SCC
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}}_{[q]_{x}}^{\prime}
(that is, one without edges leading to states not on itself).

Fix a state
q_{0}\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
.
Consider the automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
obtained from
\mathcal{A}
by removing states in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}\setminus S_{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}}
, and redirecting transition that go to
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}\setminus S_{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}}
in
\mathcal{A}
to transitions towards
q_{0}
.
For these redirected transitions, we keep the same priority if it is
\leq x
, and set it to
x
otherwise. Formally:

•

The set of states of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is
Q^{\prime}=Q\setminus\left({\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}\setminus S_{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}}\right)
.

•

The initial state is
q_{\mathsf{init}}
, or
q_{0}
if
q_{\mathsf{init}}\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}\setminus S_{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}}
.

For
q^{\prime}\in Q^{\prime}
:

•

If
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:y}p
in
\mathcal{A}
and
p\notin{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
, then
q\xrightarrow{a:y}p
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

•

If
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:y}p
in
\mathcal{A}
,
p\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}\setminus S_{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}}
, and
y\leq x
, then
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:y}q_{0}
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

•

If
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:y}p
in
\mathcal{A}
,
p\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}\setminus S_{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}}
, and
y>x
, then
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:x}q_{0}
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

For transitions in the two latter cases, we say that
q^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:y}q_{0}
has been
redirected
from

.

Remark 180
.

If
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}=S_{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}}
, then
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}=\mathcal{A}
.

The following lemma will be use to show that we can compute
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
in polynomial time, to prove the correctness of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
, and to obtain that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
is

-polished
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.

Lemma 182
.

Automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
can be computed in polynomial time from
\mathcal{A}
.

Proof.

To obtain
S_{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}}
, we first build a finite representation of the restriction of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}}_{[q]_{x}}
to
neutral letters
(we recall that, in general,
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{A}}_{[q]_{x}}
might have an infinite number of transitions).
One way of doing that is to build the following graph
G
: for each pair of states
q_{1},q_{2}\in{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
and each
y>x
, we put an edge
q_{1}\xrightarrow{y}q_{2}
if there is a path from
q_{1}
to
q_{2}
producing
y
as minimal priority and not passing trough another state in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
. By Lemma
181
,
S_{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}}
is a subgraph of
G
. To obtain the states in
S_{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}}
we just need to perform a decomposition in
SCCs
of
G
and take a
final SCC
of it.
13
13

13

If
W
is not
positional
, the procedure described here does provide a set of states
S_{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}}
, but it might lead to an incorrect automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
. If our objective is to decide the
positionality
of
W
, at the end of the procedure we need to check the equality
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A})}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime})}
; if it does not hold, we can conclude that
W
is not
positional
.
∎

We consider
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
equipped with the preorders
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{0}},\dots,\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\leq}_{x}}
inherited from
\mathcal{A}
.

Lemma 183
.

Automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-nice transformation of
\mathcal{A}
at level
x
.

Proof.

We first note that, by Lemma
171
,
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
is
[0,x-1]
-faithful
in
\mathcal{A}
, so it makes sense to speak of a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-nice transformation at level
x
.

Automaton
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\left.\kern-1.2pt\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\mathchoice{\vphantom{\big|}}{}{}{}\right|_{{\geq}x+1}}}
coincides with the
subautomaton
of
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\left.\kern-1.2pt\mathcal{A}\mathchoice{\vphantom{\big|}}{}{}{}\right|_{{\geq}x+1}}}
induced by states in
Q^{\prime}
.
Indeed, let
q_{1}^{\prime},q_{2}^{\prime}\in Q^{\prime}
and
q_{1}^{\prime}\xrightarrow{a:>x}q_{2}^{\prime}
in
\mathcal{A}
. As these states are in
Q^{\prime}
,
q_{2}^{\prime}\notin{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}\setminus S_{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}}
, so the transition has not been
redirected
, and it appears in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
. Conversely, all transitions producing a priority
>x
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
appear in
\mathcal{A}
.

We show that
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
is
[0,x-1]
-faithful
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\begin{matrix}[l]\phantom{.}\\[-2.56073pt]
{\sim_{x-1}}\\[-0.56905pt]
\hskip-4.55244pt{{{{{\leq}x-1}}}}\end{matrix}$}}\right.}}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\begin{matrix}[l]\phantom{.}\\[-2.56073pt]
{\sim_{x-1}}\\[-0.56905pt]
\hskip-4.55244pt{{{{{\leq}x-1}}}}\end{matrix}$}}\right.}}
.
Let
p_{1},p_{2}\in Q^{\prime}
such that
p_{1}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}p_{2}
, and let
p_{1}\xrightarrow{a:y_{1}^{\prime}}q_{1}^{\prime}
and
p_{2}\xrightarrow{a:y_{2}^{\prime}}q_{2}^{\prime}
be two transitions in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.
Transitions that have not been
redirected
satisfy the congruence requirements, as they satisfy them in
\mathcal{A}
.
Assume that the first of these transitions have been redirected from
p_{1}\xrightarrow{a:y_{1}}q_{1}
in
\mathcal{A}
. We have that
q_{1}^{\prime}=q_{0}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}q_{1}
, so,
q_{1}^{\prime}\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}q_{2}^{\prime}
by the congruence property in
\mathcal{A}
.
If
y_{1}^{\prime}<x
, then
y_{1}=y_{1}^{\prime}
and the
y_{1}
-uniformity
of transitions in
\mathcal{A}
yields
y_{1}^{\prime}=y_{2}^{\prime}
.
Therefore, we also have that
y_{1}^{\prime}\geq x
if and only if
y_{2}^{\prime}\geq x

This gives both the
[0,x-1]
-faithfulness
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
and the equality of the
quotient
automata.

As
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}

refines

\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{\mathcal{A}}}
, the latter relation is also a
congruence
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\sim_{\mathcal{A}}$}}\right.}}={\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}{\raisebox{1.00006pt}{$\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$\hskip-2.84526pt}\left/\hskip-1.42262pt\raisebox{-1.00006pt}{{\scriptsize$\sim_{\mathcal{A}}$}}\right.}}
.
∎

Claim 185
.

For each
i\geq 1
, the word
w_{i}a_{i}
belongs to
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[q]_{x}}^{+}
and is a
super word for

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}W_{[q]_{x}}}
.

{claimproof}

{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
in
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
producing no priority
<x
. Since
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is a
\mathrel{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\sim}_{x}}
-nice transformation at level
x
,
word
w_{i}a_{i}
also connects states in
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
in
\mathcal{A}
, without producing priorities
<x
. Therefore, it belongs to
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}\Sigma}_{[q]_{x}}^{+}
.

∎

This lemma allows us to conclude. We have obtained a deterministic automaton
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
that is
equivalent
to
\mathcal{A}
. We claim that
|\mathcal{A}^{\prime}|<|\mathcal{A}|
.
Indeed, if this was not the case, we would have that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}=S_{{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}}
, so, by Remark
180
,
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
. By the previous Lemma
186
this implies that
{\color[rgb]{0.0195,0.2109,0.2539}[q]_{x}}
was already
x
-polished
in
\mathcal{A}
, a contradiction.

Discussion: Why not just continue polishing?

We have just showed a method to
x
-polish
a given class of
\mathcal{A}
. The natural continuation would be to
polish
the rest of classes, until obtaining an
x
-polished automaton
, and then apply the first case.
The main difficulty is that the polishing operation we have presented might break the
normality
of
\mathcal{A}
.
Normality
of automata is key in all the process
(see for example Lemma
178
), so we cannot guarantee to be able to continue polishing the classes of
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
.
We would need to be able to either show that
\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
is in
normal form
(for example, by having an analogous to Lemma
176
), or to show that we can
normalise

\mathcal{A}^{\prime}
while maintaining the properties of being an
(x-2)
-structured signature automaton
.
We have not succeeded in ensuring these properties, although we believe that it should be possible to do so.
